findings.title: Knife job paths skip the dry-run gating used by every sibling path
findings.evidence: processItemJob gates the sagaCatalog follow-up enqueue on dryRun at line 509 and the autmog enqueue at line 704, but the knifeVariationBatch archive reconciliation at line 600, the knifeVariation sync at line 626, and its unconditional enqueueImageJobs call at line 655 pass no dry-run control.
findings.impact: A dry-run drain that is documented to report canonical mutations without writes can still archive knife listings and enqueue real tmp image upload and delete jobs, which the next cron run then executes. The dry-run contract is silently inconsistent per source.
findings.recommendation: Pass dryRun through syncGrimsmoKnifeVariation and reconcileGrimsmoKnifeVariationBatch and skip the enqueueImageJobs call when set, matching the autmog and saga paths, or document in the queue decision note why knife paths are exempt.

findings.title: Enqueue lock spins on a tight unbounded poll loop
findings.evidence: The do-while loop acquires the 30-second enqueue lock with SET NX PX 30000 and retries every 10 ms with no attempt cap, no backoff, and no failure path; enqueueMany repeats it serially for every job in a batch.
findings.impact: When another process holds the lock, each duplicate enqueue fires roughly 3000 Redis SET commands over up to 30 seconds and blocks the five-minute cron run for that whole window. A wedged or contended lock degrades every later queue operation in the run instead of failing fast.
findings.recommendation: Cap the lock wait (for example 5 seconds with 100 ms backoff) and return accepted false or reject on timeout so the cron run can log and continue, instead of an unbounded spin.

findings.title: Bounded drain silently force-closes after a hardcoded five minutes
findings.evidence: process() arms a 5 * 60 * 1000 setTimeout that calls finish(true), force-closing the worker and resolving with whatever partial stats exist. QueueProcessOptions exposes no timeout field, so callers cannot size the cap to their batch.
findings.impact: A large image batch with slow uploads ends mid-flight: active jobs are abandoned, BullMQ marks them stalled for a later retry, and the processor logs a normal completion with truncated counts. Operators cannot tell a capped drain from a finished one.
findings.recommendation: Make the cap an option on QueueProcessOptions, log an explicit warning when the timeout fires, and document that truncated jobs retry on the next cron tick.

findings.title: Drained event ends the bounded drain while delayed retries are pending
findings.evidence: The drain resolves when the worker emits drained, which fires when no jobs are waiting. Jobs in the delayed retry state with a 30-second exponential backoff are not waiting, so the drain closes the worker while retries are pending and the in-memory adapter shows the same behavior by processing only waiting jobs.
findings.impact: A run whose jobs failed their first attempt returns failed counts but never reaches the requested limit of terminal outcomes in that run; the retries land on the next five-minute tick. The contract in QueueProcessOptions calls the limit a target of terminal outcomes, which this run does not meet.
findings.recommendation: Document the drain-at-least-once-per-tick behavior next to QueueProcessOptions, or have the bounded drain also wait until delayed counts drop or the limit is reached before closing the worker.

findings.title: Integration contract suite hard-fails without a local redis-server binary
findings.evidence: beforeAll unconditionally spawns redis-server on a free port and waits for its readiness banner; there is no guard that skips the suite when the binary is missing.
findings.impact: pnpm test inside packages/queue fails with a spawn error on any machine or CI runner without redis-server installed, rather than skipping the transport integration and running the rest of the contract suite.
findings.recommendation: Probe for the redis-server binary first and use vitest skip when it is absent, or document the CI prerequisite next to the package test script.

findings.title: Unbounded lock retry loop can hang every enqueue during a Redis outage
findings.evidence: enqueue acquires a per-job SET NX lock in a do/while loop with no attempt cap or timeout (lines 190-201), and the shared connection is created with maxRetriesPerRequest: null (line 36). When Redis is unreachable, the queued SET command never resolves and the loop never exits; enqueueMany awaits enqueues sequentially (lines 249-255).
findings.impact: A Redis outage stalls runAutmogProducer/runGrimsmoProducer forever instead of failing: the 10ms polling loop spins, later jobs in a batch never enqueue, and with restartPolicyType NEVER the cron process never recovers or logs a failure. The replaced addBulk path errored out instead of hanging.
findings.recommendation: Bound the acquisition: after a fixed deadline or attempt count, reject with a clear error so the cron drain can log and retry on the next schedule. A short lock TTL check around the SET (e.g. a total wait budget of a few seconds) is enough; no new machinery is needed.

findings.title: Enqueue acceptance is verified through an undocumented BullMQ telemetry round-trip
findings.evidence: accepted is computed as stored?.opts.telemetry?.metadata === enqueueToken (lines 219-228), relying on BullMQ persisting the telemetry option passed to queue.add and returning it from getJob.
findings.impact: If the installed bullmq version strips or reshapes the telemetry option in persisted job opts, every successful enqueue reports accepted: false while the job is durable. Callers reading accepted (the contract exposes it) then miscount enqueued jobs; the integration contract test would catch this, but only for the happy path it asserts.
findings.recommendation: Treat queue.add completing without error as accepted (BullMQ is the source of truth for the write), and drop the second getJob round-trip and telemetry comparison; that also removes one Redis command from the hot enqueue path.

findings.title: New shared queue's persistence path is not provably attached to the retained volume
findings.evidence: The pocket-trash-queue startCommand writes RDB and AOF to $RAILWAY_VOLUME_MOUNT_PATH with --save 60 1 --appendonly yes --appendfsync everysec, but the IaC file declares redis-volume (lines 51-56) and the database as independent resources with no attach shown; the resources array (line 117) lists both separately.
findings.impact: If the Railway template does not attach redis-volume to the new database, persistence writes land on ephemeral container disk and queue state is lost on every redeploy - the AOF/RDB migration step would pass a restart test only by luck. The docs claim the template provides redis-volume, which this evidence cannot confirm.
findings.recommendation: Attach the volume explicitly to pocket-trash-queue in the IaC (or capture the generated plan output proving the attachment) before the migration stages run, so the reviewed plan shows the data path end to end.

findings.title: Scraper process now holds two Redis connections instead of one

findings.impact: Each cron run opens one extra Redis connection on the shared pocket-trash-queue instance now also serving the Discord bot. Cost is small at the current scale (one replica, */5 cron), but it doubles per-process connections against a shared capacity pool.
findings.recommendation: Either accept it and note the extra connection in docs/railway.md, or let createBullMqQueueAdapter accept an existing connection. BullMQ duplicates connections internally for workers, so the simpler fix is documentation.

findings.title: In-memory continuous worker busy-loops when handler fails without backoff
findings.evidence: After a drain, processMemoryJobs re-queues via queueMicrotask(wake) whenever any job is still waiting (lines 428-430). A handler failure with no backoff config moves the job back to waiting (line 667), so wake reschedules immediately with zero delay.
findings.impact: Test-only adapter: with retry.attempts high and no backoff, each failing job spins the microtask queue at full CPU until attempts are exhausted, starving anything else on the event loop. Scraper queues always configure backoff, so this needs an unusual definition to bite.
findings.recommendation: Only re-wake when a waiting job exists that was not just retried, or apply a minimal next-run delay when a failure left a job waiting. One condition change in wake is enough.

review.overview: PR #403 stages a shared Railway Redis queue and moves the scraper onto a new transport-independent queue package. The new packages/queue package defines a typed QueueAdapter contract with a BullMQ production adapter and a deterministic in-memory test adapter. Producers now enqueue through enqueueScraperJobs with deterministic job IDs, the processor drains item and image queues through the shared contract, and Railway provisions a second Redis instance with AOF persistence while keeping the legacy scraper queue running. The scraper itself still points REDIS_URL at the legacy queue via preserve(), so the shared queue is provisioned but not yet wired in.

findings.title: BullMQ drain counts every failed attempt, so the batch limit stops the drain early
findings.evidence: worker.on("failed", ...) increments stats.failed on every failed attempt. With retry attempts set to 5 for scraper queues, one job that always throws adds up to 5 to stats.failed inside a single process() call, while the in-memory adapter in index.ts counts exactly 1 failed per drain.
findings.impact: A bounded drain with limit N stops after N failed attempts, not N jobs. A batch of 20 jobs where 4 jobs fail all 5 attempts ends the drain with 16 jobs never picked up. Processor stats also report attempts, not jobs, so scraper-run records overstate failures. Tests run against the in-memory adapter, which counts per job, so this divergence is invisible in CI.
findings.recommendation: Count one terminal outcome per job id in the worker event handlers, or count only terminal BullMQ states (use the 'failed' event's final-attempt flag pattern). Align the in-memory adapter to whatever semantic is chosen and add a contract test where attempts is greater than 1 and the handler always fails.

findings.title: Spin-wait enqueue lock has no retry cap or timeout
findings.evidence: The do/while loop calls SET NX every 10 ms until it acquires the lock. The lock has a 30-second lease. If a holder crashes mid-lease or many processes contend on the same job id, each waiter spins for up to 30 seconds issuing roughly 3000 SET commands. enqueueMany is serial, so a whole batch pays this per contended job.
findings.impact: The scraper cron runs every 5 minutes. A contended or orphaned lock can make the producer burn its whole cron window busy-waiting and add thousands of pointless Redis round trips per job.
findings.recommendation: Bound the acquisition attempts (for example 10 with a 200 ms sleep) and return accepted false or throw on timeout. The 30-second lease already bounds correctness; only the retry loop needs a cap.

findings.title: Redis outage makes queue operations hang forever instead of failing
findings.evidence: maxRetriesPerRequest is null and retryStrategy returns null after 3 attempts, so once Redis drops, ioredis buffers commands indefinitely. enableReadyCheck is false, so no startup check catches a dead Redis either. createScraperJobContext in jobs.ts pings only the separate cron Redis connection, not the adapter's connection.
findings.impact: If Redis restarts or the network drops mid-run, the cron producer or processor hangs instead of erroring. Railway's restart policy is NEVER for the scraper, so the run stalls until the 5-minute process() timeout or forever in the enqueue path, and the scraper-run record stays open.
findings.recommendation: Retry a bounded number of times and throw when the connection is lost, or keep maxRetriesPerRequest null but set a command timeout. Also ping the adapter's connection in createScraperJobContext alongside the cron connection.

findings.title: Hardcoded 5-minute timeout force-closes active jobs mid-handler
findings.evidence: The timeout calls finish(true), which calls worker.close(true) and abandons active jobs. Scraper handlers write to the database and upload images, and retry backoff is 30 seconds exponential with 5 attempts, so a normal retry cycle can exceed 5 minutes.
findings.impact: An abandoned job is moved back to waiting while its handler may still be mid-write, so a retry can duplicate a database sync or an image upload. The timeout is not configurable, so slow batches cannot extend it.
findings.recommendation: Make the timeout an option on QueueProcessOptions with a default, and on timeout resolve with current stats instead of force-closing, or at minimum document that force-close plus retry can duplicate handler side effects.

findings.title: In-memory adapter never retries a failed job inside one bounded drain
findings.evidence: processMemoryJobs snapshots the waiting list once, then on handler failure sets the job back to waiting or delayed with retryAt. The snapshot loop never revisits it, so the job is only retried on a later process() call. The BullMQ worker retries delayed jobs inside the same drain.
findings.impact: The contract test 'reports matching attempt numbers and retries continuous jobs' passes for the memory adapter only because processContinuously re-wakes. Bounded drains behave differently across adapters: a flaky handler completes on the BullMQ path but stays waiting on the memory path. Tests validate the wrong adapter behavior.
findings.recommendation: Loop processMemoryJobs until no waiting job is eligible (respecting the terminal-outcome limit), or re-run promoteDueRetries with a batched loop. Then the shared contract tests cover both adapters truthfully.

findings.title: Enqueue acceptance check races with job state changes
findings.evidence: After queue.add, enqueue re-fetches the job and compares a telemetry metadata token to decide accepted. If a competing process removes or completes the job between add and getJob, getJob may return null or a different state and accepted becomes false even though the job was persisted.
findings.impact: A producer can record accepted false for a job that was actually enqueued, skewing enqueued-count logging and scraper-run stats. The re-fetch also adds a round trip per job in a serial enqueueMany loop.
findings.recommendation: Treat the awaited queue.add result as durable acceptance and drop the re-fetch, or only use the token check when add throws. Keep replacedCompleted from the pre-check, which is already lock-protected.

findings.title: Railway shared queue is provisioned but not reachable from scraper configuration
findings.evidence: The scraper service uses REDIS_URL: preserve(), and the deploy workflow patch sets only RAILPACK_INSTALL_CMD. Nothing in this PR points REDIS_URL at the new pocket-trash-queue instance whose endpoint is private-network-pocket-trash-queue.
findings.impact: The scraper and Discord bot keep using the legacy scraper-queue Redis until someone manually edits the variable. That matches the changeset wording 'stage ... while retaining the legacy scraper queue', but a reader of the infra alone cannot tell if the omission is deliberate.
findings.recommendation: If this is intentional staging, add a follow-up line to docs/railway.md naming the switch step and the verification checklist (queue counts migrate, legacy drains empty). If not, set REDIS_URL to the shared queue reference in the deploy workflow.

review.overview: This PR introduces a comprehensive Pens catalog schema supporting configurable pen products, refill management, and evidence-based catalog claims. The schema adds 45+ new tables spanning product details (pens, pen parts, refills), configuration management (slots, choices, rules), collection ownership, and source evidence tracking. Complex deferred constraint triggers enforce subtype consistency, configuration validity, and evidence requirements across market scopes.

findings.title: Complex deferred triggers may cause cascading validation failures
findings.evidence: The validate_pens_product_detail function uses COALESCE(NEW.id, OLD.id) which returns NULL on DELETE operations, causing the trigger to silently skip validation. The function declares target_id but then queries using WHERE p.id = target_id without checking for NULL, which could allow orphaned subtype records when parent products are deleted.
findings.impact: Deleting a product may leave orphaned records in product_detail_pen, product_detail_pen_part, and related tables because the deferred trigger may not execute validation on DELETE cascades.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit NULL check for target_id at the start of validate_pens_product_detail and validate_pens_collection_detail functions, or use TG_OP to handle DELETE operations correctly.

findings.title: Missing index on collection_item_configuration_selection foreign key
findings.evidence: Table collection_item_configuration_selection has foreign key installed_part_collection_item_id referencing collection_item(id) but no explicit index is created. This column is used in JOIN conditions within validate_collection_configuration_selections function.
findings.impact: Queries validating installed part constraints will perform sequential scans on collection_item_configuration_selection, causing performance degradation as collection sizes grow.
findings.recommendation: Add CREATE INDEX collection_item_configuration_selection_installed_part_idx ON collection_item_configuration_selection(installed_part_collection_item_id) to the migration.

findings.title: Recursive CTE in market conflict triggers may not scale
findings.evidence: The validate_refill_market_conflicts function uses a recursive CTE reach that traverses the entire catalog_market_containment graph on every INSERT or UPDATE to refill_offering_market_status or refill_offering_identifier tables.
findings.impact: As the market hierarchy grows, each write operation will trigger a full graph traversal, potentially causing write amplification and degraded write performance.
findings.recommendation: Consider materializing market ancestry paths or adding a depth limit check. Document expected market hierarchy depth constraints in AGENTS.md.

findings.title: Composite foreign key on product_detail_refill may fail with default identity
findings.evidence: The product_detail_refill table defines a composite foreign key (id, makerId) referencing product(id, makerId). The makerId column is populated via SELECT from product in the migration, but the Drizzle schema marks it as notNull without a default.
findings.impact: Applications inserting product_detail_refill rows via Drizzle must explicitly provide makerId even though it is already defined on the parent product, creating a potential for data inconsistency.
findings.recommendation: Either make makerId optional in the Drizzle schema and rely on the composite FK, or add a database trigger to auto-populate makerId from the parent product on insert.

findings.title: Constraint trigger validate_product_configuration has unreachable validation path
findings.evidence: The validate_product_configuration function checks for mismatched slot kinds but does not validate that slot_id in product_configuration_choice actually belongs to the stated product_id, allowing cross-product slot assignments.
findings.impact: A malicious or buggy insert could associate a choice with a slot from a different product, breaking the product-scoped configuration integrity.
findings.recommendation: Add a CHECK constraint or trigger validation ensuring product_configuration_choice.slot_id matches the product_id of the parent slot.

findings.title: Typo in comment referencing pen_nose_profile namespace
findings.evidence: The comment on penNoseProfileAssignment says Nose profile assigned to a Pen or Pen-tip product but the namespace check constraint is hardcoded to pen-nose-profile which does not match the comment casing.
findings.impact: Minor documentation inconsistency that may confuse developers reading the schema.
findings.recommendation: Update the comment to match the exact namespace value used in the constraint.

review.overview: PR #354 adds a normalized Pens catalog schema: 45 new tables for pen and pen-part product subtypes, refill offerings and market lifecycle, refill compatibility, product configuration, terminology concepts, source listings, and append-only evidence. It reworks catalog_terminology_alias from a product-type slug FK to a concept FK, seeds new product types, mechanisms, concepts, slot kinds, and a global market, and enforces the new invariants with deferred PL/pgSQL constraint triggers. The database layer is well built and broadly tested; the main problems are that the services layer still cannot represent the new pen product types, and two smaller integrity gaps in the offering identifier and migration seeds.

findings.title: Service layer cannot represent the new Pens product types
findings.evidence: catalogProductType() at index.ts:252-262 only accepts slider, slider-insert, slider-plate, spinner, and spinner-button, but the migration (migration.sql:497-504) seeds product types pen, pen-clip, pen-tip, pen-top-cap, pen-mechanism, pen-actuator, and refill, and seeds a terminology concept for every product type (migration.sql:514-523). createTerminologyAlias narrows the input key through this function (index.ts:2425), so pens aliases are rejected. listTerminologyAliases maps every row through it (index.ts:3613), the product read mapper calls it on the persisted slug (index.ts:8328), and the collection item mapper does the same (index.ts:9086).
findings.impact: Terminology aliases cannot be created for the exact domain this PR introduces, and any pen or refill product row makes existing read paths throw 'Unsupported catalog product type'. createProduct looks the type up by slug at runtime (index.ts:2986-2991), so an untyped caller can already create such a row and break product and collection reads.
findings.recommendation: Extend CatalogProductType and catalogProductType() with the seven seeded slugs, or replace the hardcoded union with a lookup against product_types so newly seeded types work without editing the service.

findings.title: Global terminology aliases are valid in the schema but invisible in the listing
findings.evidence: catalog_terminology_alias.maker_id is now nullable (collection.ts:580-583) and the new check only requires a maker for preferred rows (collection.ts:618-620), but listTerminologyAliases inner-joins maker on maker_id (index.ts:3600-3603), which silently drops every maker-less alias row. The 'row.makerId === null' guard at index.ts:3609-3610 can never execute because the inner join already removed those rows.
findings.impact: A non-preferred alias with no maker is accepted by the database but never appears in the admin list, so the list quietly drifts from the table contents.
findings.recommendation: Either left-join maker and return a nullable makerName for global aliases, or revert maker_id to NOT NULL until global aliases are an actual feature.

findings.title: Migration overwrites existing catalog rows and skips an audit before installing the subtype trigger
findings.evidence: The product_types seed uses ON CONFLICT (slug) DO UPDATE (migration.sql:505-508), which renames and reclassifies any row that already uses a pens slug, and the mechanisms seed does the same (migration.sql:509-513). The alias table gets a pre-migration collision audit (migration.sql:486-496), but products already typed with a colliding slug get no audit or backfill before product_pens_detail_consistent (migration.sql:762-764) starts requiring detail rows.
findings.impact: On a database that already has products under such a slug, the migration silently relabels them and the next update of those products fails at commit with 'requires product_detail_pen' or 'requires product_detail_refill'.
findings.recommendation: Add the same DO-block audit for pre-existing pens-typed products (fail the migration instead of mutating them) and prefer ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for the seed rows.

findings.title: refill_offering.normalized_tip_size is not validated against tip_size
findings.evidence: The refill_offering check (pens.ts:589-592) only verifies normalized_tip_size is a lowercase 1-80 character string. Unlike product_detail_refill_normalized_model_valid (pens.ts:153-156), nothing requires normalized_tip_size to equal lower(trim(tip_size)).
findings.impact: Rows ('0.5 mm', 'x') and ('0.5 MM', '0.5 mm') both pass the checks, so one real tip size can appear as two distinct offerings and refill_offering_identity_unique stops deduplicating them.
findings.recommendation: Extend the check to 'normalized_tip_size = lower(trim(tip_size))', matching the refill model check.

findings.title: refill_offering_identifier.maker_id is not tied to the refill's maker
findings.evidence: refill_offering_identifier.maker_id references makers (pens.ts:1038-1040) but no foreign key or trigger compares it to the maker of the offering's refill product, whose own maker_id is pinned to product.maker_id by the composite FK (pens.ts:139-143). validate_refill_successors (migration.sql:1000-1006) only preserves the maker across successor rows.
findings.impact: A maker code or SKU can be recorded against a maker that does not make the refill, and refill_offering_identifier_active_unique then blocks the real maker from registering the same code in that market.
findings.recommendation: Add a deferred trigger requiring identifier.maker_id to match the refill product's maker, or document why foreign-maker identifiers are allowed.

findings.title: Identifier successor-scope rule has no test
findings.evidence: validate_refill_successors enforces that a superseding identifier preserves maker, kind, and market (migration.sql:1001-1005), but pens-catalog.integration.test.ts only exercises the market-status branch (pens-catalog.integration.test.ts:337-348); the identifier branch is never hit.
findings.impact: A regression in the identifier scope check would pass the current test suite.
findings.recommendation: Add one expectRejectedTransaction that supersedes an identifier with a row from a different market and expects the 'Offering-identifier successor must preserve maker, kind, and market' error.

review.overview: This PR creates a new shared `@package/queue` package with a transport-independent queue abstraction and migrates the scraper to use it. The package provides both an in-memory adapter for tests and a BullMQ adapter for production. The infrastructure change provisions a new shared Redis queue alongside the legacy scraper queue for gradual migration.

findings.title: BullMQ enqueue lock may spin-wait indefinitely
findings.evidence: The enqueue method uses a busy-loop with `setTimeout(resolve, 10)` when lock acquisition fails. If Redis is slow or the lock holder crashes without releasing, this could spin indefinitely.
findings.impact: Under Redis pressure or partial outage, enqueue calls may hang forever, consuming event loop resources and never resolving.
findings.recommendation: Add a maximum retry count or timeout to the lock acquisition loop. Consider using Redis Redlock or a deadline-based approach.

findings.title: enqueueMany processes sequentially, not batched
findings.evidence: enqueueMany loops with `for (const input of inputs) results.push(await this.enqueue(input))`, making N round-trips to Redis for N jobs.
findings.impact: Large batches will be slow and create unnecessary Redis traffic. The in-memory adapter has the same pattern.
findings.recommendation: Document this as a known limitation, or implement true batching with BullMQ's `addBulk` method for production.

findings.title: BullMQ worker timeout is hardcoded to 5 minutes
findings.evidence: The process() method has `const timeout = setTimeout(..., 5 * 60 * 1_000)` with no configuration option.
findings.impact: Long-running job batches will be force-terminated even if they are making progress. This limits the usable batch size.
findings.recommendation: Make the timeout configurable via QueueProcessOptions, or document the 5-minute limit clearly in the contract.

findings.title: Shared queue Redis uses different persistence settings than legacy
findings.evidence: Shared queue has `--appendonly yes --appendfsync everysec` while legacy uses no AOF. The volume is shared between both Redis instances.
findings.impact: If both queues mount the same volume, they will corrupt each other's data. If separate volumes, the shared queue has durability but legacy does not.
findings.recommendation: Verify the shared queue has its own volume. Document why AOF is enabled for shared but not legacy.

findings.title: In-memory adapter pruneRetained sorts completed jobs on every call
findings.evidence: pruneRetained converts the Map to an array and sorts it by completedAt on every counts() and process() call.
findings.impact: Tests with many completed jobs will get slower linearly. Production uses BullMQ, so this only affects test performance.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable for tests. Consider adding a comment noting this is O(n log n) per operation.

findings.title: Contract test does not verify telemetry token matching
findings.evidence: The enqueue method checks `stored?.opts.telemetry?.metadata === enqueueToken` to verify the job was stored correctly.
findings.impact: If BullMQ changes its telemetry structure, the accepted flag could be wrong. No test covers this verification path.
findings.recommendation: Add a contract test that mocks BullMQ's telemetry behavior to verify the token matching logic.

findings.title: Scraper processor still imports from scraper-specific paths
findings.evidence: The processor imports `@package/queue` types but also has tight coupling to scraper-specific database operations and image workflows.
findings.impact: The queue abstraction is clean, but the processor remains tied to scraper domain logic. This is expected but limits reusability.
findings.recommendation: No fix needed. The abstraction boundary is correctly placed at the queue level, not the processor level.

assessments.evidence: apps/scraper/src/queue/processor.ts:599-620 calls reconcileGrimsmoKnifeVariationBatch without dryRun parameter; lines 626-680 call syncGrimsmoKnifeVariation and enqueueImageJobs without dryRun check. Compare to line 509 where sagaCatalog gates enqueueImageJobs on dryRun, and lines 702-708 where autmog checks dryRun before enqueuing.
assessments.reason: The knife variation paths (knifeVariationBatch and knifeVariation) do not receive or respect the dryRun parameter, while sibling paths (sagaCatalog at line 509, autmog at line 704) explicitly check dryRun before enqueuing image jobs. This creates an inconsistent dry-run contract where knife jobs perform real archive reconciliations and enqueue real image upload/delete jobs even in dry-run mode.

assessments.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:190-201 shows a do-while loop acquiring a 30-second lock with SET NX PX 30000, retrying every 10ms with no attempt limit. Line 249-254 shows enqueueMany calling enqueue serially for each job in the batch.
assessments.reason: The spin loop has no cap on attempts and no backoff strategy. If another process holds the lock, this issues approximately 3000 Redis SET commands over 30 seconds. The serial enqueueMany amplifies the issue across batch jobs. This can block the cron run for the entire lock duration instead of failing fast.

assessments.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:277-282 sets a hardcoded 5-minute timeout (5 * 60 * 1000) that calls finish(true), force-closing the worker. QueueProcessOptions (referenced in index.ts) exposes no timeout configuration field.
assessments.reason: The timeout is hardcoded with no configurability. When it fires, active jobs are abandoned via force-close, BullMQ marks them stalled for retry, and the resolved stats are partial. There is no explicit warning logged when truncation occurs, making it indistinguishable from normal completion.

assessments.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:315-317 listens for the 'drained' event to resolve the process promise. BullMQ's 'drained' fires when waiting count reaches zero, but delayed jobs (exponential backoff retries) are in a separate 'delayed' state, not 'waiting'.
assessments.reason: Jobs that fail and enter a delayed retry state (30-second exponential backoff) do not count as 'waiting'. The drained event fires while these retries are pending, causing the worker to close before delayed jobs return to waiting state. The limit option targets terminal outcomes (completed/failed/skipped), but delayed retries haven't reached terminal state yet.

assessments.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.integration.test.ts:13-23 shows beforeAll unconditionally calling spawn('redis-server', ...) with no guard for binary absence. There is no conditional skip or prerequisite check.
assessments.reason: The test suite unconditionally attempts to spawn redis-server. If the binary is not installed, spawn throws an error and the test suite fails hard rather than skipping. This prevents the contract tests from running in environments without Redis installed, even though the remaining test suite could pass.

assessments.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:190-201 (review-evidence/29-content.txt): lock is acquired with `SET ... PX 30_000 NX`, sleep is 10ms per retry; ioredis client at lines 33-46.
assessments.reason: The unbounded loop is real, but both stated hang scenarios are wrong. A crashed lock holder is not indefinite: the lock expires after 30 seconds (PX 30_000, line 194), so the wait is bounded by ~TTL plus one 10ms retry. A 10ms setTimeout poll does not meaningfully consume event loop resources. If Redis is slow or down, the `await this.#connection.set` itself hangs regardless of the loop (maxRetriesPerRequest: null, line 36) — the lock loop adds nothing. No supported path to 'spin forever' at the claimed severity.

assessments.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:249-255 (29-content.txt:253): `for (const input of inputs) results.push(await this.enqueue(input))`. Each enqueue performs ~5 sequential Redis round-trips (SET NX at 191, getJob at 204, add at 220, getJob at 224, EVAL at 231). Used for image batches via enqueueScraperJobs (apps/scraper/src/queue/queues.ts:334-338, 19-content.txt).
assessments.reason: Confirmed sequential: N jobs cost roughly 5N sequential Redis round-trips. In-memory adapter has the same pattern (31-content.txt:377-381). review.overview: This PR establishes a transport-independent queue boundary by creating a new @package/queue package that abstracts BullMQ behind a typed contract. findings.title: Enqueue lock polling loop lacks backoff ceiling
findings.evidence: The lock acquisition loop uses a fixed 10ms delay with no maximum retry count: `await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));`
findings.impact: Under Redis contention or network issues, this could create hundreds of round-trips per enqueue, consuming connection pool resources and increasing latency without bound.
findings.recommendation: Add a maximum retry limit (e.g., 50 attempts = 500ms) and escalate to an error if the lock cannot be acquired, or use exponential backoff with a ceiling.

findings.title: enqueueMany processes jobs sequentially
findings.evidence: The implementation iterates and awaits each enqueue: `for (const input of inputs) results.push(await this.enqueue(input));`
findings.impact: Large batches will have O(n) latency. For a batch of 100 jobs, this means 100 sequential Redis round-trips instead of parallel execution.
findings.recommendation: Consider using Promise.all with a concurrency limit (e.g., p-limit) to parallelize enqueue operations while maintaining result order alignment.

findings.title: Redis connection errors silently swallowed
findings.evidence: The error handler is empty: `connection.on("error", () => { // The operation waiting on Redis surfaces connection failures. });`
findings.impact: Connection failures at startup or during operation may not be visible in logs until an operation times out, making debugging difficult.
findings.recommendation: Log connection errors with structured context (at minimum the error message) to enable observability of Redis health issues.

findings.title: Lock token cleanup failure ignored
findings.evidence: The eval for lock cleanup is wrapped in try/catch with empty catch: `try { await this.#connection.eval(...) } catch { // The lease expires... }`
findings.impact: While the lock has a TTL, consistent failures to clean up could accumulate stale keys and increase Redis memory usage.
findings.recommendation: Log cleanup failures at debug level so they can be monitored without alerting, or track cleanup success metrics.

findings.title: BullMQ worker timeout hardcoded to 5 minutes
findings.evidence: The bounded process timeout is fixed: `const timeout = setTimeout(..., 5 * 60 * 1_000);`
findings.impact: Long-running jobs or slow handlers may exceed this timeout and be force-closed mid-processing.
findings.recommendation: Consider making the timeout configurable per-queue or deriving it from retry.backoff settings.

findings.title: Worker force-close timeout hardcoded
findings.evidence: Force close timeout is fixed at 30 seconds: `setTimeout(() => void worker.close(true).finally(resolve), 30_000)`
findings.impact: Handlers requiring longer graceful shutdown will be force-closed, potentially leaving jobs in an inconsistent state.
findings.recommendation: Make the graceful shutdown timeout configurable in QueueProcessOptions.

findings.title: Legacy queue Redis lacks AOF persistence
findings.evidence: The legacy scraper-queue uses `save 60 1` only, while the new pocket-trash-queue adds `--appendonly yes --appendfsync everysec`.
findings.impact: During the migration period, the legacy queue could lose up to 60 seconds of data on unclean shutdown versus ~1 second for the new queue.
findings.recommendation: Document this difference in the migration runbook and prioritize cutover to minimize exposure.

review.overview: This PR introduces a transport-independent queue abstraction layer via the new @package/queue package. It creates a shared Railway Redis queue (pocket-trash-queue) staged alongside the legacy scraper-queue for migration. The package provides two adapters: an in-memory adapter for deterministic tests and a BullMQ adapter for production. Applications define typed queues with Zod-validated payloads, retry policies, retention settings, and deduplication rules. findings.title: Busy-wait lock acquisition with unbounded retry
findings.evidence: The enqueue method uses `do { ... } while (acquired !== "OK")` with only a 10ms delay. Under high concurrency, multiple processes could spin-wait indefinitely for the same lock.
findings.impact: Lock contention spikes could cause CPU thrashing and Redis connection exhaustion, degrading throughput during batch enqueue operations.
findings.recommendation: Add exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum attempt limit before failing the enqueue operation.

findings.title: Redis EVAL unlock could fail silently
findings.evidence: The Lua script for lock cleanup swallows all errors with an empty catch block. If the Redis connection is flaky, locks could persist beyond the 30s TTL.
findings.impact: Stale locks delay job enqueueing until TTL expiration, causing unnecessary duplicate prevention and queue processing delays.
findings.recommendation: Log lock cleanup failures at debug level to enable diagnosis without affecting the enqueue outcome.

findings.title: enqueueMany processes jobs sequentially
findings.evidence: The enqueueMany implementation loops with `for (const input of inputs) results.push(await queue.enqueue(input))`, acquiring a lock for each job serially.
findings.impact: Large batches enqueue slower than necessary. With the lock acquisition overhead, a 1000-job batch could take significant time.
findings.recommendation: Document this behavior as intentional for correct duplicate result alignment, or implement batch-aware locking if throughput becomes a concern.

findings.title: Process timeout hardcoded to 5 minutes
findings.evidence: The bounded process method sets a fixed 5-minute timeout. Jobs exceeding this duration trigger forced worker closure.
findings.impact: Long-running scraper jobs (e.g., large image uploads) could be interrupted mid-processing, leaving jobs in an inconsistent state.
findings.recommendation: Make the timeout configurable in QueueProcessOptions with a safe default, or derive it from job count and expected processing time.

findings.title: Lock TTL shorter than max retry delay
findings.evidence: The enqueue lock TTL is 30 seconds, but scraper queue retry policy uses exponential backoff with 30s initial delay and up to 5 attempts.
findings.impact: If a job fails and retries with delays, the lock could expire before the retry completes, allowing duplicate job creation.
findings.recommendation: Extend the lock TTL to exceed the maximum possible retry duration (30s * 2^4 = 480s) or make it configurable per queue.

findings.title: Telemetry metadata comparison for enqueue verification
findings.evidence: Enqueue success is verified by comparing `stored?.opts.telemetry?.metadata === enqueueToken`. This relies on BullMQ internal structure.
findings.impact: BullMQ version upgrades could change the telemetry structure, causing false negatives where jobs are accepted but reported as failed.
findings.recommendation: Use a custom job property or Redis verification instead of internal BullMQ fields for enqueue confirmation.

findings.title: Continuous worker lacks backpressure handling
findings.evidence: processContinuously creates a worker without explicit queue depth limits or backpressure signaling.
findings.impact: If job production exceeds processing capacity, the queue could grow unbounded, exhausting Redis memory.
findings.recommendation: Add optional queue depth monitoring and pause/resume controls to the QueueWorker interface for backpressure management.

review.overview: This PR adds a comprehensive Pens catalog schema supporting pen products, refill compatibility tracking, and evidence-based catalog management. It introduces 42 new tables including product subtypes (pens, pen parts, refills), collection tracking for owned items, configuration slots and choices for customizable products, refill offerings with market-aware versioning, and an evidence system for audit trails. The implementation uses PostgreSQL-specific features including deferred constraint triggers, complex CHECK constraints, and recursive CTEs for market graph validation. The schema is well-tested with 371 lines of integration tests covering constraint validation.

findings.title: Complex CHECK constraint may impact query planning and maintainability
findings.evidence: The refill_compatibility_evidence_fields_valid constraint uses a 43-line complex conditional with nested num_nonnulls() calls checking mutually exclusive field groups across 4 different evidence kinds
findings.impact: This complex expression makes the query planner's job harder and increases risk of subtle bugs when the evidence kinds evolve. It also limits PostgreSQL's ability to use constraint exclusion.
findings.recommendation: Split this into separate CHECK constraints for each evidence kind using PostgreSQL 16's ability to have multiple constraints, or consider using a table-per-kind pattern if the validation logic diverges further.

findings.title: Recursive CTE in market conflict validation risks performance degradation
findings.evidence: validate_refill_market_conflicts uses recursive CTEs with multiple JOINs to detect market containment cycles and conflicts across refill_offering_market_status and refill_offering_identifier tables
findings.impact: This deferred trigger runs on every insert/update to market status, identifiers, or market containment. With deep market hierarchies or high write volume, this will cause noticeable latency.
findings.recommendation: Add a materialized path or closure table for market hierarchies to replace recursive CTEs with indexed lookups, or at minimum add a depth limit to prevent unbounded recursion.

findings.title: Source evidence URL lacks format validation
findings.evidence: catalog_source_evidence.original_url is defined as text NOT NULL without CHECK constraint for URL format validation
findings.impact: Invalid URLs can be stored that may cause downstream failures when the evidence system attempts to fetch or display them.
findings.recommendation: Add a CHECK constraint using regex pattern matching for URL validation: check('catalog_source_evidence_url_valid', sql`original_url ~* '^https?://'`)

findings.title: Missing indexes on critical lookup paths
findings.evidence: collection_detail_pen table has indexes on product_pen_id and installed_refill_product_id but no composite index for the common query pattern of finding a user's pens by installed refill
findings.impact: Queries that join collection_detail_pen with product_detail_refill for a specific user's collection will require index merging or sequential scans.
findings.recommendation: Add a composite index on (installed_refill_product_id, product_pen_id) or ensure the query planner can efficiently use existing indexes through index-only scans.

findings.title: Destructive migration operations on existing table
findings.evidence: Migration drops constraints on catalog_terminology_alias (lines 483-485), runs an audit query, then re-adds constraints (lines 571). If this migration fails mid-way, the table is left without constraints.
findings.impact: Partial migration failure could leave the terminology alias table without uniqueness constraints, allowing duplicate data that breaks application assumptions.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the entire catalog_terminology_alias transformation in a single transaction block, or use a safer pattern: add new columns first, populate them, then drop old columns in a separate migration.

findings.title: Composite foreign key may cause ORM relation inference issues
findings.evidence: collection_detail_pen has a composite FK to refill_offering on (installed_refill_offering_id, installed_refill_product_id) requiring both columns match
findings.impact: Drizzle ORM may struggle to properly infer the many-to-one relationship for this composite key, leading to type errors or requiring manual relation configuration.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit relation configuration in relations.ts for this composite key relationship, or consider denormalizing to use a single surrogate key if the composite nature isn't strictly required by business rules.

findings.title: Missing RLS policies for new catalog tables
findings.evidence: None of the 42 new tables in pens.ts have Row Level Security (RLS) policies defined, though the existing codebase pattern in collection.ts uses RLS for privacy control
findings.impact: Access control must be enforced entirely at the application layer, increasing risk of data exposure if queries are written without proper filtering.
findings.recommendation: Consider adding RLS policies for tables like catalog_source_evidence, refill_compatibility_assertion, and collection_detail_pen that contain sensitive or user-specific data.

findings.title: No explicit transaction isolation test for concurrent modifications
findings.evidence: 371 lines of integration tests cover constraint validation but no test verifies behavior under concurrent transactions or serialization failures
findings.impact: Race conditions in deferred constraint validation or market conflict detection may not surface until production load.
findings.recommendation: Add a test that runs two concurrent transactions attempting to create conflicting market status entries to verify proper serialization.

review.overview: This PR introduces a comprehensive Pens catalog schema with 40+ new tables supporting configurable pen products, refill compatibility tracking, market-specific offerings, and evidence-based assertions. findings.title: Complex trigger validation may cause performance issues at scale
findings.evidence: The validate_pens_product_detail trigger performs multiple SELECT count(*) queries against subtype tables on every product modification, and validate_refill_market_conflicts uses recursive CTEs for market reachability checks
findings.impact: Deferred constraint triggers execute at commit time; bulk operations on pens or refills could experience significant slowdowns as data grows
findings.recommendation: Consider benchmarking with realistic data volumes; monitor query plans for the recursive CTEs in market conflict detection

findings.title: Missing composite index on refill_compatibility_assertion for common lookup pattern
findings.evidence: Table has indexes on individual foreign keys but the primary query pattern (pen_product_id + required_tip_product_id + target_refill_product_id) requires a composite index that exists, but the target_group variant is missing similar coverage
findings.impact: Queries filtering by pen and tip without refill may not use optimal index paths
findings.recommendation: Verify query patterns against actual execution plans; consider adding covering indexes for the most frequent join paths

findings.title: collection_item_configuration_selection lacks foreign key to product_configuration_slot for slot_id
findings.evidence: The slot_id column references productConfigurationSlot.id in the composite FK but the FK only validates (choice_id, slot_id) pairs, not direct slot ownership
findings.impact: Could allow orphaned slot references if choice validation is bypassed
findings.recommendation: Add direct FK from slot_id to product_configuration_slot.id if not already covered by check constraints

findings.title: refill_compatibility_evidence has no index on test_date for temporal queries
findings.evidence: The test_date column is used in physical-fit-test evidence kind but lacks dedicated indexing; queries filtering by date ranges will scan
findings.impact: Evidence audits and reports filtered by test date will perform poorly
findings.recommendation: Add index on test_date if temporal filtering is a planned access pattern

findings.title: catalog_source_evidence append-only trigger prevents corrections
findings.evidence: The keep_catalog_source_evidence_append_only trigger raises exception on any UPDATE or DELETE, even for admin corrections
findings.impact: Data entry errors in source evidence cannot be fixed without disabling triggers or recreating rows
findings.recommendation: Consider soft-delete pattern or admin bypass for legitimate corrections

findings.title: Pen part role assignment allows duplicate roles per part
findings.evidence: pen_part_role_assignment primary key is (part_product_id, concept_id) but different concepts with same key in different namespaces could assign multiple roles to one part
findings.impact: A pen part could have conflicting functional roles if terminology concepts are misconfigured
findings.recommendation: Consider enforcing single role per part at the application layer

findings.title: Configuration choice position validation allows gaps
findings.evidence: Position is checked >= 0 but not for sequential uniqueness; gaps in choice positions within a slot are allowed
findings.impact: UI may display choices with unexpected ordering gaps
findings.recommendation: Verify UI handles non-sequential positions correctly

review.overview: This PR adds material Trends drill-downs to the existing Trends feature. It introduces a new `public_collection_item_material_trend` table for privacy-safe collection-derived material counts, adds exact catalog-product material counts via raw SQL with grouping sets, and implements frontend filtering by general and specific materials. The feature supports both headline aggregates and drill-down breakdowns by material type and specific alloy/grade.

findings.title: Coalesce unique index may collide with real ID 0
findings.evidence: The unique index uses `coalesce("product_type_id", 0)` which treats NULL and 0 as the same value. If ID 0 ever exists in product_types, this index would incorrectly reject valid inserts.
findings.impact: Data integrity risk if the referenced tables ever contain ID 0, causing unique constraint violations on legitimate data.
findings.recommendation: Use a sentinel value outside the normal ID range (like -1) or use PostgreSQL's NULLS NOT DISTINCT feature if available.

findings.title: Row key generation creates ambiguous keys
findings.evidence: The `rowKey` function concatenates values: `${value.productTypeId ?? "all"}:${value.materialId ?? "unspecified"}:${value.materialSpecificId ?? "general"}:${value.isSpecificBreakdown}`. If materialId is null (unspecified) and productTypeId is also null (all), the key pattern overlaps with valid combinations.
findings.impact: React key collisions could cause incorrect re-rendering or component state issues when multiple rows produce identical keys.
findings.recommendation: Include an explicit discriminator like a static prefix or use JSON.stringify with the full object to guarantee uniqueness.

findings.title: Material filter clears specific selection on general change
findings.evidence: When a new material is selected, the code clears `materialSpecificId: undefined` unconditionally. This prevents preserving the specific material when switching between materials that share the same specific options.
findings.impact: Users lose their specific material selection when changing general materials, even if the new material has the same specific options available.
findings.recommendation: Preserve the specific material selection if the new material also has that specific option available, only clearing when incompatible.

findings.title: Empty material options still renders select
findings.evidence: The material Select renders even when `materialOptions` is empty, showing only the 'All materials' option with no actual choices.
findings.impact: Confusing UI when no materials have associated Trends data - users see a filter with no meaningful options.
findings.recommendation: Conditionally render the material filter only when `materialOptions.length > 0` to hide irrelevant controls.

findings.title: Catalog material trends not filtered by stale status
findings.evidence: Collection material Trends show a stale warning based on `collectionMaterialTrends.stale`, but catalog material Trends have no equivalent freshness indicator even though they come from the same generation refresh cycle.
findings.impact: Users may see outdated catalog counts without any indication that the data is stale.
findings.recommendation: Add a staleness indicator for catalog material Trends or document that catalog counts are always real-time.

findings.title: Composite foreign key columns not individually nullable-safe
findings.evidence: The composite foreign key on `(materialId, materialSpecificId)` references `material_specific(material_id, id)`. While the check constraint ensures `materialSpecificId` implies `materialId`, the Drizzle ORM types allow `materialSpecificId` to be set while `materialId` is null at compile time.
findings.impact: Type system gap could allow runtime foreign key violations that TypeScript cannot catch.
findings.recommendation: Add a branded type or conditional type that requires `materialId` when `materialSpecificId` is provided.

review.overview: Adds material drill-downs to the public Trends page. A new privacy-safe table stores rounded item and collector counts per generation, product type, material, and alloy, gated by a five-collector threshold and rounded to the nearest five. The refresh job aggregates owned collection items with grouping sets; a separate query returns exact catalog-product material counts. The web app gains material and alloy URL filters, two new server functions, a wider route loader, and three new chart sections. Integration, page, and route tests plus a Storybook drill-down story are included.

findings.title: Specific-material lookups join on id alone, ignoring the composite key
findings.evidence: The catalog query joins material_specific on material_specific.id = scoped_products.material_specific_id (line 185), and getPublicCollectionMaterialTrends left-joins schema.materialSpecific on materialSpecificId = materialSpecific.id (lines 250-255). The PR's own foreign key in packages/database/src/schema/trends.ts (lines 98-102) identifies a specific row by (material_id, id), and the migration references material_specific(material_id, id), so that pair must be the unique key.
findings.impact: If two materials carry the same specific id, each trend row matches two material_specific rows. The public page then shows the wrong alloy name, links to the wrong material page, or lists the same bucket twice in both the exact catalog and privacy-safe charts.
findings.recommendation: Add material_id to both joins: material_specific.material_id = row.material_id and material_specific.id = row.material_specific_id, plus the matching eq pair in the drizzle leftJoin. Add an integration fixture with two materials sharing one specific id; the current fixture only creates one material.

findings.title: Refresh stores invisible breakdown rows for the Unspecified bucket
findings.evidence: The finer grouping set (product_type_id, material_id, material_specific_id) also groups items whose product has no material, producing rows with material_id null, material_specific_id null, and isSpecificBreakdown true. The catalog query's grouping sets (lines 186-188) produce the same rows.
findings.impact: The UI can never show these rows: the general view requires isSpecificBreakdown false, and the drill-down requires a non-null materialId. They bloat every generation, and if one falls below the contributor threshold it sets hasSuppressedMaterialValues true even though nothing visible was suppressed, so the page shows the suppressed notice for no reason.
findings.recommendation: Drop rows with materialId null and isSpecificBreakdown true before the insert and from the catalog result, or restrict the finer grouping set to items that have a material.

findings.title: Alloy dropdown offers options that produce an empty chart
findings.evidence: materialSpecificOptions collects specific rows for the selected material from all product-type scopes, but filterMaterials (line 227) keeps only rows whose productTypeId equals the current selection, which is null when all product types are shown.
findings.impact: An alloy that occurs only on part-or-accessory product types is absent from headline rows, because the headline excludes those types. Selecting it while product type is all yields an empty chart and the generic empty message.
findings.recommendation: Build materialSpecificOptions from rows matching the current productTypeId, the same condition filterMaterials applies.

review.overview: This PR adds a normalized Pens catalog schema to the database package: about 45 tables covering pen and pen-part product subtypes, refill models and offerings, compatibility groups and assertions, product configuration slots and choices, markets, source listings, and append-only evidence. Terminology aliases move from product-type slug keys to a general concept registry, with a collision preflight guarding the backfill in the migration. Integrity lives in deferred constraint triggers, seed data ships in the migration, and the services, tests, and generated schema diagram were adapted. I assumed admin-scale writes, not bulk imports; the trigger table scans are fine at that scale.

findings.title: Terminology alias service cannot read or write the new concept namespaces
findings.evidence: The migration drops the catalog_terminology_alias_namespace_valid check (migration line 485) and seeds concepts for the new pen product types and for non product-type namespaces. But catalogProductType (line 252) only accepts the five legacy spinner and slider slugs and throws otherwise. listTerminologyAliases maps every row through it at line 3613 with no namespace filter, and createTerminologyAlias calls it at line 2425.
findings.impact: Admins cannot create maker aliases for the new Pen, Pen Clip, or Refill product types even though the migration seeds their concepts; the create call throws Unsupported catalog product type. Any alias row in a non product-type namespace, which the schema now permits, makes listTerminologyAliases throw for every caller. Rows that pass the key check are returned with canonicalNamespace hardcoded to product-type regardless of their real namespace.
findings.recommendation: Filter the list query to canonicalNamespace = product-type until other namespaces are supported, and add the new pen slugs to the CatalogProductType union or carry the concept key as a plain string for the new types.

findings.title: Pen and spinner detail rows can mix on one product or collection item
findings.evidence: validate_pens_collection_detail counts only the six collection_detail_pen tables (lines 780 to 787) and validate_pens_product_detail counts only pen family tables. The fresh baseline seed shows products of an unrelated type accepting product_detail_spinner rows, so no visible constraint rejects cross family details. collection_catalog_product unions all detail families with LIMIT 1 and no ORDER BY (lines 918 to 931).
findings.impact: A collection item or product can hold detail rows from both the pen family and the spinner or slider family. The catalog product mapping then returns an arbitrary one of the two products, so configuration selection validation checks the wrong product and pages can show mixed subtype data.
findings.recommendation: Extend both validators to also count the pre-existing spinner and slider detail tables, or add one shared exactly-one-detail constraint across all families. Give collection_catalog_product a deterministic order or raise when more than one family matches.

findings.title: Collection selection trigger and several rule rejections have no tests
findings.evidence: The suite covers subtype deferral, required slots, rule ordering, market cycles, and evidence support. No test inserts into collection_item_configuration_selection, so validate_collection_configuration_selections (installed part owner match, single install, slot product match) is untested. No test rejects a choice whose carrier does not match its slot kind, and no test rejects two rules with the same requirement set even though the third test title says it does.
findings.impact: The most complex trigger in the migration can break silently. The carrier kind check, the duplicate rule signature check, and the whole owned part installation flow have no test that fails when they break.
findings.recommendation: Add rejection cases: a material choice in an appearance slot, a second rule for the same target with the same requirement set, a selection whose slot belongs to another product, an installed part owned by another user, and the same part installed twice.

findings.title: Global aliases are legal in the schema but invisible to the alias list
findings.evidence: The migration drops NOT NULL on catalog_terminology_alias.maker_id (line 566) and the new scope unique uses NULLS NOT DISTINCT, so global aliases are legal. listTerminologyAliases inner joins maker on alias.maker_id at line 3600, which drops those rows before the null guard at line 3609 can ever fire.
findings.impact: A legal global alias is invisible in the only list endpoint and the guard throw is dead code. The schema and the service disagree about whether global aliases exist.
findings.recommendation: Pick one side. If global aliases are planned, left join maker and make makerName nullable in the response. If not, keep maker_id NOT NULL and drop the nullsNotDistinct unique.

findings.title: Four redundant unique constraints add write cost with no integrity gain
findings.evidence: pens.ts declares four unique constraints already implied by narrower ones: product_configuration_choice_id_slot_product_unique at line 416, product_configuration_choice_rule_id_target_product_unique at line 472, refill_offering_market_status_id_scope_unique at line 980, and refill_offering_identifier_id_scope_unique at line 1058. Each includes the identity primary key column and no composite foreign key references these column sets.
findings.impact: Four extra unique indexes are maintained on every insert and update of the choice, rule, status, and identifier tables with no integrity gain.
findings.recommendation: Delete the four constraints from pens.ts and regenerate the migration. Keep only the key pairs that composite foreign keys actually reference.

review.overview: PR #354 adds a normalized Pens catalog to the database package: 43 new tables in one Drizzle migration (product and collection pen subtypes, refill offerings, market-scoped lifecycle and identifier versioning, compatibility assertions, append-only source evidence), a matching pens.ts Drizzle schema, a large relations graph, and a remodel of catalog_terminology_alias from a product-type slug key to a new concept table with a pre-backfill collision audit. The catalog service create/list alias paths were reworked for the new conceptId column. A 371-line PGlite integration test covers the deferred triggers (subtype consistency, configuration carrier rules, market graph conflicts, evidence requirements, successor scope). The design leans on deferred per-row constraint triggers that validate whole-table state at commit, which keeps insert order flexible but makes every changed row rescan the table set.

findings.title: Per-row market conflict triggers rescan the whole market graph for every changed row
findings.evidence: validate_refill_market_conflicts is a DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED FOR EACH ROW constraint trigger (lines 1131-1133). Each firing rebuilds a recursive reach CTE over all of catalog_market and self-joins refill_offering_market_status or refill_offering_identifier across the entire table, regardless of which row changed.
findings.impact: An import that inserts N market-status or identifier rows in one transaction fires the function N times, each doing a full recursive-graph rebuild plus a full-table self-join. A few thousand rows turns into minutes of quadratic work at commit. The same whole-table-per-row pattern exists in validate_refill_supporting_evidence (line 1012) and validate_collection_configuration_selections (line 933), but those scan smaller tables.
findings.recommendation: Keep the triggers for online admin edits, but scope each EXISTS check to the rows touched by the current statement (filter on the triggering row's offering_id or maker_id instead of scanning all rows), or document that bulk imports must run in small batches per transaction.

findings.title: A collection item can hold one Pens detail and one pre-existing spinner or slider detail
findings.evidence: validate_pens_collection_detail counts only the six collection_detail_pen* tables and requires that sum to be exactly 1. It never checks collection_detail_spinner, collection_detail_spinner_button, collection_detail_slider, collection_detail_slider_plate, or collection_detail_slider_insert, which collection_catalog_product (line 918) unions over.
findings.impact: If no pre-existing constraint guards cross-family exclusivity, an item with both a pen detail and a spinner detail passes. collection_catalog_product then picks between the two products with LIMIT 1 and no order, so collection_item_configuration_selection gets validated against an arbitrary product. The evidence for this PR does not include the earlier migrations, so the pre-existing guard could not be confirmed.
findings.recommendation: Extend the count in validate_pens_collection_detail to include the pre-existing detail families (or confirm an existing trigger already enforces one detail per item across families) and add a test that an item with a pen detail plus a spinner detail is rejected.

findings.title: Successor chains can form cycles because a superseded row may point at another superseded row
findings.evidence: The successor CHECKs (lines 441 and 464) only require successor_id to be non-null, different from the row's own id, and scope-preserving. validate_refill_successors (lines 991-1008) also only checks scope. Nothing stops A.superseded_at = t1, A.successor_id = B and B.superseded_at = t2, B.successor_id = A.
findings.impact: Code that walks successor_id to find the active market status or identifier can loop forever, or silently resolve to a superseded row. Both rows are inactive, so the partial unique indexes do not catch this.
findings.recommendation: In validate_refill_successors, also require the successor row to have superseded_at is null. That keeps chains linear and finite, and forces the app to repoint predecessors when it supersedes a middle row.

findings.title: listTerminologyAliases silently hides maker-less global aliases and its null guard is dead code
findings.evidence: The query inner joins maker on catalog_terminology_alias.makerId (lines 3600-3603). This PR makes makerId nullable and adds the scope unique constraint with NULLS NOT DISTINCT, so global aliases are a supported row shape. An inner join filters those rows out before the map runs, so the throw at line 3609 can never execute.
findings.impact: Once a global alias is inserted outside this service (the schema and migration explicitly allow it), it disappears from the admin list with no error. The guard meant to catch that case never fires.
findings.recommendation: Left-join maker and decide explicitly: either return global aliases with makerId null, or filter them with a documented where clause, and delete the unreachable throw.

findings.title: Terminology collision rule is bypassed when a concept label is renamed
findings.evidence: validate_catalog_terminology_aliases rejects an alias whose normalized_value equals a concept key or label, but the constraint trigger fires only on INSERT OR UPDATE of catalog_terminology_alias. The concept-side trigger (line 842) only enforces key and namespace immutability.
findings.impact: Updating catalog_terminology_concept.normalized_canonical_label to a value that collides with an existing alias's normalized_value is accepted. The invariant the alias trigger enforces no longer holds after a concept rename.
findings.recommendation: Fire validate_catalog_terminology_aliases on UPDATE of catalog_terminology_concept as well, since labels are mutable while keys are not.

findings.title: refill_tip_style and refill_ink_color accept blank or unbounded name and slug values
findings.evidence: Both tables declare name and slug as plain text NOT NULL with only uniqueness constraints (lines 523-535 and 538-550). Every peer lookup table in this PR, such as configuration_slot_kind, adds char_length(trim(...)) between 1 and 80 checks on the same kind of columns.
findings.impact: A slug of a single space or a multi-megabyte name is accepted. A whitespace slug passes the unique index and then breaks slug-based lookups or URLs downstream.
findings.recommendation: Add the same length and trim checks used by configuration_slot_kind to both tables.

A new exact endpoint counts approved public catalog products by general material and specific alloy, and the existing privacy-safe refresh now also stores owned-item and collector counts per material, using the same 5-contributor threshold and round-to-five rule as the existing product-type trends. findings.title: material_specific is joined on id alone, contradicting the composite identity this change declares
findings.evidence: The catalog query joins left join material_specific on material_specific.id = scoped_products.material_specific_id (line 185), and the collection reader left joins materialSpecific on materialSpecific.id alone (lines 250-256). The new foreign key in packages/database/src/schema/trends.ts (lines 98-102) instead references material_specific(material_id, id), and every existing API in catalog-api.ts (product materialAssignments lines 398-402, saveAdminMaterialSpecific lines 1825-1831, moveAdminMaterialImage lines 1852-1859) identifies a specific by the materialId plus specificId pair.
findings.impact: If specific ids repeat across materials, as the composite foreign key and pair-based APIs imply, both queries fan out. The catalog grouping emits duplicate rows for one bucket with conflicting names and slugs, the collection reader returns one stored row many times with wrong labels, and the page renders duplicate React keys and wrong View products links. If ids are globally unique, the current joins happen to work.
findings.recommendation: Join on both columns in both queries: add and material_specific.material_id = scoped_products.material_id to the raw SQL, and pair the eq for the Drizzle left join. findings.title: Collection material rows have no defined order; a test asserts one anyway
findings.evidence: The rows select in getPublicCollectionMaterialTrends (lines 226-262) has no orderBy, while sibling reads order by descending count then ascending name (lines 332-335). The integration test at packages/services/src/db/trends/index.integration.test.ts (lines 95-106) asserts an exact array order, Steel before Titanium, two rows with the same count 10.
findings.impact: Postgres may return equal-count rows in any order. That assertion can flake after a restore or plan change, and the page sorts only by count, so tied bars and rows can swap between page loads.

review.overview: This PR adds material Trends drill-downs to the existing Trends page. It introduces a new database table `public_collection_item_material_trend` for storing privacy-safe material trend data, service methods for querying both exact catalog material counts and privacy-safe collection material counts, and enhanced UI components for filtering and visualizing material trends with drill-down capabilities by general material and specific alloy/grade.

findings.title: Transaction rollback may leave orphaned trend data on refresh failure
findings.evidence: The refreshPublicCollectionItemTrends method performs multiple INSERT operations (product types at line 572, part accessories at line 587, materials at line 598) before the atomic generation swap. If hooks.beforeActivate throws after material inserts succeed, the transaction rolls back but any concurrent readers may briefly see partially written trend data due to the transaction isolation level.
findings.impact: Under high load with concurrent refresh operations, readers could observe inconsistent trend states where material trends exist but product-type trends do not, violating the atomic generation contract.
findings.recommendation: Move all INSERT operations into a single batch or use a staging table pattern where all trend types are written to temporary tables before the atomic swap commits.

findings.title: Composite foreign key with RESTRICT blocks material deletion
findings.evidence: The migration adds ALTER TABLE constraint `public_collection_item_material_trend_specific_parent_fk` with FOREIGN KEY (material_id, material_specific_id) REFERENCES material_specific(material_id, id) ON DELETE RESTRICT.
findings.impact: Deleting a material or material_specific that has any trend history will fail with a foreign key violation. This blocks data cleanup operations and may require manual intervention to remove old trend generations before materials can be deleted.
findings.recommendation: Change ON DELETE RESTRICT to ON DELETE CASCADE for the material_specific composite key, or implement a soft-delete pattern for materials that preserves trend history while allowing logical deletion.

findings.title: Unique index with COALESCE may not optimize equality queries
findings.evidence: The unique index `public_collection_item_material_trend_scope_unique` uses COALESCE for nullable columns: `coalesce("product_type_id", 0),coalesce("material_id", 0),coalesce("material_specific_id", 0)`.
findings.impact: Queries filtering by actual material_id values without COALESCE may not use this index efficiently, requiring sequential scans on the potentially large trend table.
findings.recommendation: Add separate partial indexes for common query patterns: `CREATE INDEX ON public_collection_item_material_trend (generation_id, material_id) WHERE material_id IS NOT NULL` to support the material filter lookups.

findings.title: URL state filter logic has subtle null vs undefined mismatch
findings.evidence: The filterMaterials function compares `value.productTypeId === (productTypeId ?? null)` where productTypeId from URL search may be undefined, but the database stores NULL for headline aggregates.
findings.impact: When no product type is selected, the filter correctly shows headline rows. However, the comparison relies on JavaScript's loose equality between undefined and null which could break if the search parser changes.
findings.recommendation: Normalize the comparison: `value.productTypeId === productTypeId || (value.productTypeId === null && !productTypeId)` for explicit handling of both undefined and null cases.

findings.title: Missing test for material-specific constraint violation
findings.evidence: The integration tests verify happy-path material trend generation but do not test the CHECK constraint `scope_valid` that prevents material_specific_id without material_id, nor the RESTRICT foreign key behavior.
findings.impact: A bug in the trend generation SQL that produces invalid material-specific rows without parent materials would only be caught at runtime in production.
findings.recommendation: Add a test case that verifies the database rejects invalid trend rows where isSpecificBreakdown=true but materialSpecificId exists without a materialId.

findings.title: Raw SQL in catalog material trends lacks type validation
findings.evidence: The getPublicCatalogMaterialTrends method uses db.execute with a raw SQL template literal containing complex GROUP BY GROUPING SETS logic. The result row mapping manually converts string|number to Number.
findings.impact: If PostgreSQL returns unexpected types (e.g., bigint as string), the manual Number() conversion could produce NaN or incorrect values without raising an error.
findings.recommendation: Add runtime validation that count values are finite positive integers before returning, or use a schema validation library to verify the query result shape.

findings.title: Refresh persists material drill-down rows that no view can render, and their suppression wrongly flags hidden values
findings.evidence: The refresh grouping set at lines 538-541 emits rows grouped by product type, material, and specific material. For items whose product has no product_material row, it emits rows with material_id null and is_specific_breakdown true. The threshold filter at lines 555-558 keeps them and the insert at lines 597-614 persists them. The same dead rows also inflate the response of getPublicCatalogMaterialTrends.
