review.overview:
Reviewer 1: This PR creates a new shared `@package/queue` package with a transport-independent queue abstraction and migrates the scraper to use it. The package provides both an in-memory adapter for tests and a BullMQ adapter for production. The infrastructure change provisions a new shared Redis queue alongside the legacy scraper queue for gradual migration.

Reviewer 2: PR #403 stages a shared Railway Redis queue and moves the scraper onto a new transport-independent @package/queue package. The package defines typed queues (payload schema, mode, retry, retention, completed-job deduplication), ships a BullMQ/ioredis production adapter plus a deterministic in-memory test adapter, and runs one shared behavioral contract suite against both. The scraper keeps its physical queue names scraper-items and scraper-images with unchanged retry and retention policy, so persisted jobs stay compatible during the migration. The Railway IaC now describes both the legacy scraper-queue Redis (retained until an approved cleanup) and a new pocket-trash-queue Redis with RDB and AOF persistence (staged, referenced by nothing yet), and the Deploy workflow continues pointing preview REDIS_URL at the legacy queue until the separately approved cutover. The changeset pair records the queue boundary and the persistence staging.

findings.title: enqueueMany processes sequentially, not batched
findings.evidence: enqueueMany loops with `for (const input of inputs) results.push(await this.enqueue(input))`, making N round-trips to Redis for N jobs.
findings.impact: Large batches will be slow and create unnecessary Redis traffic. The in-memory adapter has the same pattern.
findings.recommendation: Document this as a known limitation, or implement true batching with BullMQ's `addBulk` method for production.

findings.title: BullMQ worker timeout is hardcoded to 5 minutes
findings.evidence: The process() method has `const timeout = setTimeout(..., 5 * 60 * 1_000)` with no configuration option.
findings.impact: Long-running job batches will be force-terminated even if they are making progress. This limits the usable batch size.
findings.recommendation: Make the timeout configurable via QueueProcessOptions, or document the 5-minute limit clearly in the contract.

findings.title: In-memory adapter pruneRetained sorts completed jobs on every call
findings.evidence: pruneRetained converts the Map to an array and sorts it by completedAt on every counts() and process() call.
findings.impact: Tests with many completed jobs will get slower linearly. Production uses BullMQ, so this only affects test performance.
findings.recommendation: Acceptable for tests. Consider adding a comment noting this is O(n log n) per operation.

findings.title: Scraper processor still imports from scraper-specific paths
findings.evidence: The processor imports `@package/queue` types but also has tight coupling to scraper-specific database operations and image workflows.
findings.impact: The queue abstraction is clean, but the processor remains tied to scraper domain logic. This is expected but limits reusability.
findings.recommendation: No fix needed. The abstraction boundary is correctly placed at the queue level, not the processor level.

findings.title: Knife job paths skip the dry-run gating used by every sibling path
findings.evidence: processItemJob gates the sagaCatalog follow-up enqueue on dryRun at line 509 and the autmog enqueue at line 704, but the knifeVariationBatch archive reconciliation at line 600, the knifeVariation sync at line 626, and its unconditional enqueueImageJobs call at line 655 pass no dry-run control.
findings.impact: A dry-run drain that is documented to report canonical mutations without writes can still archive knife listings and enqueue real tmp image upload and delete jobs, which the next cron run then executes. The dry-run contract is silently inconsistent per source.
findings.recommendation: Pass dryRun through syncGrimsmoKnifeVariation and reconcileGrimsmoKnifeVariationBatch and skip the enqueueImageJobs call when set, matching the autmog and saga paths, or document in the queue decision note why knife paths are exempt.

findings.title: Enqueue lock spins on a tight unbounded poll loop
findings.evidence: The do-while loop acquires the 30-second enqueue lock with SET NX PX 30000 and retries every 10 ms with no attempt cap, no backoff, and no failure path; enqueueMany repeats it serially for every job in a batch.
findings.impact: When another process holds the lock, each duplicate enqueue fires roughly 3000 Redis SET commands over up to 30 seconds and blocks the five-minute cron run for that whole window. A wedged or contended lock degrades every later queue operation in the run instead of failing fast.
findings.recommendation: Cap the lock wait (for example 5 seconds with 100 ms backoff) and return accepted false or reject on timeout so the cron run can log and continue, instead of an unbounded spin.

findings.title: Bounded drain silently force-closes after a hardcoded five minutes
findings.evidence: process() arms a 5 * 60 * 1000 setTimeout that calls finish(true), force-closing the worker and resolving with whatever partial stats exist. QueueProcessOptions exposes no timeout field, so callers cannot size the cap to their batch.
findings.impact: A large image batch with slow uploads ends mid-flight: active jobs are abandoned, BullMQ marks them stalled for a later retry, and the processor logs a normal completion with truncated counts. Operators cannot tell a capped drain from a finished one.
findings.recommendation: Make the cap an option on QueueProcessOptions, log an explicit warning when the timeout fires, and document that truncated jobs retry on the next cron tick.

findings.title: Drained event ends the bounded drain while delayed retries are pending
findings.evidence: The drain resolves when the worker emits drained, which fires when no jobs are waiting. Jobs in the delayed retry state with a 30-second exponential backoff are not waiting, so the drain closes the worker while retries are pending and the in-memory adapter shows the same behavior by processing only waiting jobs.
findings.impact: A run whose jobs failed their first attempt returns failed counts but never reaches the requested limit of terminal outcomes in that run; the retries land on the next five-minute tick. The contract in QueueProcessOptions calls the limit a target of terminal outcomes, which this run does not meet.
findings.recommendation: Document the drain-at-least-once-per-tick behavior next to QueueProcessOptions, or have the bounded drain also wait until delayed counts drop or the limit is reached before closing the worker.

findings.title: Integration contract suite hard-fails without a local redis-server binary
findings.evidence: beforeAll unconditionally spawns redis-server on a free port and waits for its readiness banner; there is no guard that skips the suite when the binary is missing.
findings.impact: pnpm test inside packages/queue fails with a spawn error on any machine or CI runner without redis-server installed, rather than skipping the transport integration and running the rest of the contract suite.
findings.recommendation: Probe for the redis-server binary first and use vitest skip when it is absent, or document the CI prerequisite next to the package test script.

A 10ms setTimeout poll does not meaningfully consume event loop resources. If Redis is slow or down, the `await this.#connection.set` itself hangs regardless of the loop (maxRetriesPerRequest: null, line 36) — the lock loop adds nothing. No supported path to 'spin forever' at the claimed severity.

review.overview:
Reviewer 1: This PR introduces a transport-independent queue abstraction layer via the new @package/queue package. It creates a shared Railway Redis queue (pocket-trash-queue) staged alongside the legacy scraper-queue for migration. The package provides two adapters: an in-memory adapter for deterministic tests and a BullMQ adapter for production. Applications define typed queues with Zod-validated payloads, retry policies, retention settings, and deduplication rules. The scraper app migrates from direct BullMQ usage to the new abstraction while maintaining backward-compatible queue names and job IDs.

Reviewer 2: PR #403 stages a shared Railway Redis queue and moves the scraper onto a new transport-independent queue package. The new packages/queue package defines a typed QueueAdapter contract with a BullMQ production adapter and a deterministic in-memory test adapter. Producers now enqueue through enqueueScraperJobs with deterministic job IDs, the processor drains item and image queues through the shared contract, and Railway provisions a second Redis instance with AOF persistence while keeping the legacy scraper queue running. The scraper itself still points REDIS_URL at the legacy queue via preserve(), so the shared queue is provisioned but not yet wired in.

findings.title: Process timeout hardcoded to 5 minutes
findings.evidence: The bounded process method sets a fixed 5-minute timeout. Jobs exceeding this duration trigger forced worker closure.
findings.impact: Long-running scraper jobs (e.g., large image uploads) could be interrupted mid-processing, leaving jobs in an inconsistent state.
findings.recommendation: Make the timeout configurable in QueueProcessOptions with a safe default, or derive it from job count and expected processing time.

findings.title: BullMQ drain counts every failed attempt, so the batch limit stops the drain early
findings.evidence: worker.on("failed", ...) increments stats.failed on every failed attempt. With retry attempts set to 5 for scraper queues, one job that always throws adds up to 5 to stats.failed inside a single process() call, while the in-memory adapter in index.ts counts exactly 1 failed per drain.
findings.impact: A bounded drain with limit N stops after N failed attempts, not N jobs. A batch of 20 jobs where 4 jobs fail all 5 attempts ends the drain with 16 jobs never picked up. Processor stats also report attempts, not jobs, so scraper-run records overstate failures. Tests run against the in-memory adapter, which counts per job, so this divergence is invisible in CI.
findings.recommendation: Count one terminal outcome per job id in the worker event handlers, or count only terminal BullMQ states (use the 'failed' event's final-attempt flag pattern). Align the in-memory adapter to whatever semantic is chosen and add a contract test where attempts is greater than 1 and the handler always fails.

findings.title: Spin-wait enqueue lock has no retry cap or timeout
findings.evidence: The do/while loop calls SET NX every 10 ms until it acquires the lock. The lock has a 30-second lease. If a holder crashes mid-lease or many processes contend on the same job id, each waiter spins for up to 30 seconds issuing roughly 3000 SET commands. enqueueMany is serial, so a whole batch pays this per contended job.
findings.impact: The scraper cron runs every 5 minutes. A contended or orphaned lock can make the producer burn its whole cron window busy-waiting and add thousands of pointless Redis round trips per job.
findings.recommendation: Bound the acquisition attempts (for example 10 with a 200 ms sleep) and return accepted false or throw on timeout. The 30-second lease already bounds correctness; only the retry loop needs a cap.

findings.title: Redis outage makes queue operations hang forever instead of failing
findings.evidence: maxRetriesPerRequest is null and retryStrategy returns null after 3 attempts, so once Redis drops, ioredis buffers commands indefinitely. enableReadyCheck is false, so no startup check catches a dead Redis either. createScraperJobContext in jobs.ts pings only the separate cron Redis connection, not the adapter's connection.
findings.impact: If Redis restarts or the network drops mid-run, the cron producer or processor hangs instead of erroring. Railway's restart policy is NEVER for the scraper, so the run stalls until the 5-minute process() timeout or forever in the enqueue path, and the scraper-run record stays open.
findings.recommendation: Retry a bounded number of times and throw when the connection is lost, or keep maxRetriesPerRequest null but set a command timeout. Also ping the adapter's connection in createScraperJobContext alongside the cron connection.

findings.title: Hardcoded 5-minute timeout force-closes active jobs mid-handler
findings.evidence: The timeout calls finish(true), which calls worker.close(true) and abandons active jobs. Scraper handlers write to the database and upload images, and retry backoff is 30 seconds exponential with 5 attempts, so a normal retry cycle can exceed 5 minutes.
findings.impact: An abandoned job is moved back to waiting while its handler may still be mid-write, so a retry can duplicate a database sync or an image upload. The timeout is not configurable, so slow batches cannot extend it.
findings.recommendation: Make the timeout an option on QueueProcessOptions with a default, and on timeout resolve with current stats instead of force-closing, or at minimum document that force-close plus retry can duplicate handler side effects.

findings.title: In-memory adapter never retries a failed job inside one bounded drain
findings.evidence: processMemoryJobs snapshots the waiting list once, then on handler failure sets the job back to waiting or delayed with retryAt. The snapshot loop never revisits it, so the job is only retried on a later process() call. The BullMQ worker retries delayed jobs inside the same drain.
findings.impact: The contract test 'reports matching attempt numbers and retries continuous jobs' passes for the memory adapter only because processContinuously re-wakes. Bounded drains behave differently across adapters: a flaky handler completes on the BullMQ path but stays waiting on the memory path. Tests validate the wrong adapter behavior.
findings.recommendation: Loop processMemoryJobs until no waiting job is eligible (respecting the terminal-outcome limit), or re-run promoteDueRetries with a batched loop. Then the shared contract tests cover both adapters truthfully.

findings.title: Enqueue acceptance check races with job state changes
findings.evidence: After queue.add, enqueue re-fetches the job and compares a telemetry metadata token to decide accepted. If a competing process removes or completes the job between add and getJob, getJob may return null or a different state and accepted becomes false even though the job was persisted.
findings.impact: A producer can record accepted false for a job that was actually enqueued, skewing enqueued-count logging and scraper-run stats. The re-fetch also adds a round trip per job in a serial enqueueMany loop.
findings.recommendation: Treat the awaited queue.add result as durable acceptance and drop the re-fetch, or only use the token check when add throws. Keep replacedCompleted from the pre-check, which is already lock-protected.

findings.title: Railway shared queue is provisioned but not reachable from scraper configuration
findings.evidence: The scraper service uses REDIS_URL: preserve(), and the deploy workflow patch sets only RAILPACK_INSTALL_CMD. Nothing in this PR points REDIS_URL at the new pocket-trash-queue instance whose endpoint is private-network-pocket-trash-queue.
findings.impact: The scraper and Discord bot keep using the legacy scraper-queue Redis until someone manually edits the variable. That matches the changeset wording 'stage ... while retaining the legacy scraper queue', but a reader of the infra alone cannot tell if the omission is deliberate.
findings.recommendation: If this is intentional staging, add a follow-up line to docs/railway.md naming the switch step and the verification checklist (queue counts migrate, legacy drains empty). If not, set REDIS_URL to the shared queue reference in the deploy workflow.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:190-201 (review-evidence/29-content.txt) confirms the do/while SET NX retry with a 10ms sleep, but the lock is SET with PX 30_000 (line 195), so a crashed holder blocks a waiter at most ~30s; the adapter uses one shared Redis connection (line 33), and each waiter sleeps 10ms between attempts.
dispositions.reason: The code pattern is real, but the claimed impact mechanisms are factually wrong. 'Spin-wait indefinitely' is impossible: the 30s TTL bounds every wait. 'CPU thrashing' is wrong: an awaited 10ms timer is ~100 cheap wakeups/sec, not a spin. 'Redis connection exhaustion' is wrong: no new connections are created. The worst realistic case is a sub-30s delay for a contended job id, which is the intended dedup serialization. High severity is unsupported.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:229-239 shows the empty catch, but it is an intentional, commented decision ('The lease expires; cleanup must not overwrite the durable enqueue outcome'). The lock is created with PX 30_000 (line 195), so Redis guarantees expiry.
dispositions.reason: The core claim 'locks could persist beyond the 30s TTL' is factually wrong: SET PX 30_000 expires the key regardless of whether the EVAL unlock runs. Worst case of a failed unlock is that the same job id's next enqueue waits out the remaining TTL (under 30s). Swallowing the cleanup error is deliberate so a flaky connection cannot flip a durable enqueue outcome to a failure. High severity is unsupported.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:243-255 confirms sequential enqueueMany, but the doc comment on line 244 states 'Enqueues jobs in input order so duplicate results remain aligned' — a documented decision. Drain batch sizes come from SCRAPER_IMAGE_BATCH_SIZE / SCRAPER_ITEM_BATCH_SIZE, test defaults 10 and 20 (apps/scraper/src/env.test.ts:117-118, review-evidence/10-content.txt).
dispositions.reason: The code observation is accurate, but this is a commented, intentional trade-off, and the expected load does not cross it: scraper batches are tens of jobs (defaults 10-20), each a handful of Redis round trips. The hypothetical 1000-job batch does not exist in this PR. The finding's own recommendation ('document this behavior as intentional') is already satisfied by the doc comment. Medium severity is unsupported.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:277-282: setTimeout(..., 5 * 60 * 1_000) calls finish(true), which force-closes the worker and abandons active jobs. The contract type QueueProcessOptions (packages/queue/src/index.ts:140-154, review-evidence/31-content.txt) exposes only handler, concurrency, and limit — no timeout field. Scraper jobs do network-bound remote image uploads (apps/scraper/src/queue/processor.ts:827, 1063).
dispositions.reason: Verified and the impact holds. One correction: the 5-minute cap applies to the whole drain session, not a single job, but the effect is as claimed — a slow batch of image uploads can exceed it and active jobs get force-abandoned mid-flight. BullMQ's retry policy (attempts: 5) and the idempotent tmp-image flow (overwriteFile: true) soften data loss, but a hardcoded, non-configurable cap that interrupts real work is a fair medium finding.

dispositions.evidence: The enqueue lock is acquired and released entirely inside enqueue() (packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:187-240); the finally block at 229-240 deletes it before the method returns. Job retries run long after, against BullMQ's durable jobId dedup (queue.add with jobId: input.id, line 221). Retry policy is in apps/scraper/src/queue/queues.ts:23-26 (review-evidence/19-content.txt).
dispositions.reason: Category error. The 30s lock guards only the short check-then-add enqueue critical section; it is never held during job processing or retry backoff, so retry delays cannot interact with the lock TTL. Duplicate prevention after enqueue rests on BullMQ's persisted jobId, not on the lock. The claimed duplicate-creation path does not exist.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:222 and 226 confirm the telemetry metadata write-and-compare. The round trip is exercised against a real Redis + BullMQ in the integration contract test (packages/queue/src/bullmq.integration.test.ts:27-31 and test-contract assertions accepted: true at test-contract.ts:45, review-evidence/28/32-content.txt). No production caller reads result.accepted — enqueueScraperJobs only counts replacedCompleted (apps/scraper/src/queue/queues.ts:338-340).
dispositions.reason: The code claim is verified, but the impact cannot be established from the frozen source. job.opts is a public BullMQ surface and the app writes the telemetry field itself, so 'internal structure' overstates the coupling; the current behavior is pinned by an integration test that fails loudly on upgrade breakage. Whether a future BullMQ version stops persisting it is unknowable here, and even a false negative would not change production behavior since accepted is not consumed by scraper code. Low severity either way; insufficient evidence to accept the stated impact.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:331-352 confirms processContinuously creates a plain worker with no depth controls, but every production queue defined in this PR is mode: 'bounded' (apps/scraper/src/queue/queues.ts:303, 309). processContinuously has no production caller in the frozen source — only contract tests (test-contract.ts:183, 222 and contract.test.ts:85).
dispositions.reason: The code observation is accurate but there is no concrete case: nothing in this PR runs a continuous worker, so the unbounded-growth scenario has no trigger path. An unbounded queue is also the inherent nature of BullMQ queues generally; depth monitoring and pause/resume is an ops feature request, not a defect in this change. No supported impact in the frozen source.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:L311-314 shows `worker.on("failed", () => { stats.failed += 1; finishAtLimit(); })`. Each retry attempt triggers a 'failed' event before BullMQ's internal retry logic moves the job to delayed. With scraper retry policy set to 5 attempts, one permanently failing job increments stats.failed 5 times in a single process() call. The finishAtLimit() at L301 checks `stats.completed + stats.failed + stats.skipped >= options.limit`, so a batch of 20 jobs with 4 jobs failing all 5 attempts (20 failed events) would trigger the limit before processing all jobs.
dispositions.reason: Evidence supports the claim: BullMQ emits 'failed' on every attempt, not just terminal failures. The in-memory adapter at packages/queue/src/index.ts:L629 snapshots waiting jobs once and counts each job only once regardless of retries, creating a behavioral divergence. The scraper-run stats would overstate failures since they count attempts not jobs.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:L190-201 shows `do { acquired = await this.#connection.set(lockKey, lockToken, "PX", 30_000, "NX"); if (acquired !== "OK") { await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10)); } } while (acquired !== "OK");`. This loop has no iteration cap. The lock expires after 30 seconds (PX 30_000), but a crashed holder or high contention could spin ~3000 times (30s / 10ms) per waiting process. enqueueMany at L249-255 is serial, so each contended job in a batch pays this cost.
dispositions.reason: Evidence supports the claim: The do/while has no max attempts or timeout. The 30-second lease bounds correctness but not the spinning. The scraper cron runs every 5 minutes, so a stuck lock could consume the entire window.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:L33-46 shows `maxRetriesPerRequest: null` and `retryStrategy(times) { return times <= 3 ? Math.min(times * 250, 1_000) : null; }`. With maxRetriesPerRequest as null, ioredis queues commands indefinitely during a Redis outage. enableReadyCheck is false (L35), so startup doesn't validate connectivity. The retryStrategy only affects reconnection attempts, not command buffering.
dispositions.reason: Evidence supports the claim: maxRetriesPerRequest: null causes infinite command buffering. The scraper has restartPolicyType: 'NEVER' per .railway/railway.ts:L86, so a hang persists until the 5-minute process timeout or indefinitely for enqueue operations.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:L277-282 shows `const timeout = setTimeout(() => { void finish(true).then(() => resolve(stats), reject); }, 5 * 60 * 1_000);` - a hardcoded 5-minute timeout. The finish(true) at L290-298 calls `closeWorker(worker, force)` with force=true. closeWorker at L436-439 shows `if (force) { await worker.close(true); return; }`, which abandons active jobs immediately. Scraper retry backoff is 30 seconds exponential with 5 attempts (per PR context), totaling ~15 minutes worst case.
dispositions.reason: Evidence supports the claim: The 5-minute timeout force-closes via worker.close(true). Active handlers writing to database or uploading images can be interrupted mid-operation. A moved-back-to-waiting job may retry while the previous handler is still running, causing duplicate writes.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/index.ts:L627-629 shows `const waiting = [...input.jobs.values()].filter((job) => job.state === "waiting").slice(0, input.options.limit);` - a one-time snapshot. L660-674 shows on handler failure, job.state becomes 'delayed' or 'waiting' with retryAt set, but the outer loop at L631-684 only iterates over the initial waiting snapshot. The job is not revisited in the current drain.
dispositions.reason: Evidence supports the claim: processMemoryJobs snapshots waiting jobs once. Failed jobs reset to waiting/delayed are not reprocessed in the same bounded drain. BullMQ worker handles retries within the same drain cycle, creating a behavioral divergence that contract tests may mask.

dispositions.evidence: packages/queue/src/bullmq.ts:L220-226 shows `await this.#queue.add(...)` followed by `const stored = await this.#queue.getJob(input.id);` and `accepted: stored?.opts.telemetry?.metadata === enqueueToken`. If a competing process removes or completes the job between add and getJob, stored is null and accepted becomes false despite the job having been persisted.
dispositions.reason: Evidence supports the claim: The re-fetch creates a race condition. A job could be validly processed and completed between the add and getJob calls, causing accepted: false for a successfully enqueued job. This adds a redundant round trip per job in serial enqueueMany.

dispositions.evidence: .railway/railway.ts:L103 shows `REDIS_URL: preserve()` - preserving the existing value. Lines 39-49 provision a new `sharedQueue` with privateNetworkEndpoint: 'pocket-trash-queue', but nothing in the PR updates REDIS_URL to point at this new endpoint. The scraper service continues using the legacy scraper-queue Redis.
dispositions.reason: Evidence supports the claim: The shared queue is provisioned but REDIS_URL is only preserved, not redirected. The deploy workflow patch (evidence/3-patch.txt) only sets RAILPACK_INSTALL_CMD. Without explicit REDIS_URL configuration, the scraper cannot reach the new shared queue.

review.overview:
Reviewer 1: This PR introduces a comprehensive Pens catalog schema supporting configurable pen products, refill management, and evidence-based catalog claims. The schema adds 45+ new tables spanning product details (pens, pen parts, refills), configuration management (slots, choices, rules), collection ownership, and source evidence tracking. Complex deferred constraint triggers enforce subtype consistency, configuration validity, and evidence requirements across market scopes.

Reviewer 2: PR #354 adds a normalized Pens catalog schema: 45 new tables for pen and pen-part product subtypes, refill offerings and market lifecycle, refill compatibility, product configuration, terminology concepts, source listings, and append-only evidence. It reworks catalog_terminology_alias from a product-type slug FK to a concept FK, seeds new product types, mechanisms, concepts, slot kinds, and a global market, and enforces the new invariants with deferred PL/pgSQL constraint triggers. The database layer is well built and broadly tested; the main problems are that the services layer still cannot represent the new pen product types, and two smaller integrity gaps in the offering identifier and migration seeds.

findings.title: Recursive CTE in market conflict triggers may not scale
findings.evidence: The validate_refill_market_conflicts function uses a recursive CTE reach that traverses the entire catalog_market_containment graph on every INSERT or UPDATE to refill_offering_market_status or refill_offering_identifier tables.
findings.impact: As the market hierarchy grows, each write operation will trigger a full graph traversal, potentially causing write amplification and degraded write performance.
findings.recommendation: Consider materializing market ancestry paths or adding a depth limit check. Document expected market hierarchy depth constraints in AGENTS.md.

findings.title: Service layer cannot represent the new Pens product types
findings.evidence: catalogProductType() at index.ts:252-262 only accepts slider, slider-insert, slider-plate, spinner, and spinner-button, but the migration (migration.sql:497-504) seeds product types pen, pen-clip, pen-tip, pen-top-cap, pen-mechanism, pen-actuator, and refill, and seeds a terminology concept for every product type (migration.sql:514-523). createTerminologyAlias narrows the input key through this function (index.ts:2425), so pens aliases are rejected. listTerminologyAliases maps every row through it (index.ts:3613), the product read mapper calls it on the persisted slug (index.ts:8328), and the collection item mapper does the same (index.ts:9086).
findings.impact: Terminology aliases cannot be created for the exact domain this PR introduces, and any pen or refill product row makes existing read paths throw 'Unsupported catalog product type'. createProduct looks the type up by slug at runtime (index.ts:2986-2991), so an untyped caller can already create such a row and break product and collection reads.
findings.recommendation: Extend CatalogProductType and catalogProductType() with the seven seeded slugs, or replace the hardcoded union with a lookup against product_types so newly seeded types work without editing the service.

findings.title: Global terminology aliases are valid in the schema but invisible in the listing
findings.evidence: catalog_terminology_alias.maker_id is now nullable (collection.ts:580-583) and the new check only requires a maker for preferred rows (collection.ts:618-620), but listTerminologyAliases inner-joins maker on maker_id (index.ts:3600-3603), which silently drops every maker-less alias row. The 'row.makerId === null' guard at index.ts:3609-3610 can never execute because the inner join already removed those rows.
findings.impact: A non-preferred alias with no maker is accepted by the database but never appears in the admin list, so the list quietly drifts from the table contents.
findings.recommendation: Either left-join maker and return a nullable makerName for global aliases, or revert maker_id to NOT NULL until global aliases are an actual feature.

findings.title: Migration overwrites existing catalog rows and skips an audit before installing the subtype trigger
findings.evidence: The product_types seed uses ON CONFLICT (slug) DO UPDATE (migration.sql:505-508), which renames and reclassifies any row that already uses a pens slug, and the mechanisms seed does the same (migration.sql:509-513). The alias table gets a pre-migration collision audit (migration.sql:486-496), but products already typed with a colliding slug get no audit or backfill before product_pens_detail_consistent (migration.sql:762-764) starts requiring detail rows.
findings.impact: On a database that already has products under such a slug, the migration silently relabels them and the next update of those products fails at commit with 'requires product_detail_pen' or 'requires product_detail_refill'.
findings.recommendation: Add the same DO-block audit for pre-existing pens-typed products (fail the migration instead of mutating them) and prefer ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for the seed rows.

findings.title: refill_offering.normalized_tip_size is not validated against tip_size
findings.evidence: The refill_offering check (pens.ts:589-592) only verifies normalized_tip_size is a lowercase 1-80 character string. Unlike product_detail_refill_normalized_model_valid (pens.ts:153-156), nothing requires normalized_tip_size to equal lower(trim(tip_size)).
findings.impact: Rows ('0.5 mm', 'x') and ('0.5 MM', '0.5 mm') both pass the checks, so one real tip size can appear as two distinct offerings and refill_offering_identity_unique stops deduplicating them.
findings.recommendation: Extend the check to 'normalized_tip_size = lower(trim(tip_size))', matching the refill model check.

findings.title: refill_offering_identifier.maker_id is not tied to the refill's maker
findings.evidence: refill_offering_identifier.maker_id references makers (pens.ts:1038-1040) but no foreign key or trigger compares it to the maker of the offering's refill product, whose own maker_id is pinned to product.maker_id by the composite FK (pens.ts:139-143). validate_refill_successors (migration.sql:1000-1006) only preserves the maker across successor rows.
findings.impact: A maker code or SKU can be recorded against a maker that does not make the refill, and refill_offering_identifier_active_unique then blocks the real maker from registering the same code in that market.
findings.recommendation: Add a deferred trigger requiring identifier.maker_id to match the refill product's maker, or document why foreign-maker identifiers are allowed.

findings.title: Identifier successor-scope rule has no test
findings.evidence: validate_refill_successors enforces that a superseding identifier preserves maker, kind, and market (migration.sql:1001-1005), but pens-catalog.integration.test.ts only exercises the market-status branch (pens-catalog.integration.test.ts:337-348); the identifier branch is never hit.
findings.impact: A regression in the identifier scope check would pass the current test suite.
findings.recommendation: Add one expectRejectedTransaction that supersedes an identifier with a row from a different market and expects the 'Offering-identifier successor must preserve maker, kind, and market' error.

The function also has an explicit NOT FOUND guard at line 725. The orphan claim fails too: every product_detail_* table references product(id) with ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleting a product removes its detail rows, and orphaned subtype records cannot remain.

On a database with existing pens-typed products, the migration silently relabels them and subsequent updates fail with 'requires product_detail_pen' or 'requires product_detail_refill'. The product_detail_refill table enforces its maker_id matches the product's maker_id via composite FK, but the identifier table has no such validation. The validate_refill_successors trigger only checks that successors preserve the same maker, not that the identifier's maker matches the refill product's maker. review.overview:
Reviewer 1: This PR adds a comprehensive Pens catalog schema supporting pen products, refill compatibility tracking, and evidence-based catalog management. It introduces 42 new tables including product subtypes (pens, pen parts, refills), collection tracking for owned items, configuration slots and choices for customizable products, refill offerings with market-aware versioning, and an evidence system for audit trails. The implementation uses PostgreSQL-specific features including deferred constraint triggers, complex CHECK constraints, and recursive CTEs for market graph validation. The schema is well-tested with 371 lines of integration tests covering constraint validation.

Reviewer 2: This PR adds a normalized Pens catalog schema to the database package: about 45 tables covering pen and pen-part product subtypes, refill models and offerings, compatibility groups and assertions, product configuration slots and choices, markets, source listings, and append-only evidence. Terminology aliases move from product-type slug keys to a general concept registry, with a collision preflight guarding the backfill in the migration. Integrity lives in deferred constraint triggers, seed data ships in the migration, and the services, tests, and generated schema diagram were adapted. I assumed admin-scale writes, not bulk imports; the trigger table scans are fine at that scale.

findings.title: No explicit transaction isolation test for concurrent modifications
findings.evidence: 371 lines of integration tests cover constraint validation but no test verifies behavior under concurrent transactions or serialization failures
findings.impact: Race conditions in deferred constraint validation or market conflict detection may not surface until production load.
findings.recommendation: Add a test that runs two concurrent transactions attempting to create conflicting market status entries to verify proper serialization.

findings.title: Terminology alias service cannot read or write the new concept namespaces
findings.evidence: The migration drops the catalog_terminology_alias_namespace_valid check (migration line 485) and seeds concepts for the new pen product types and for non product-type namespaces. But catalogProductType (line 252) only accepts the five legacy spinner and slider slugs and throws otherwise. listTerminologyAliases maps every row through it at line 3613 with no namespace filter, and createTerminologyAlias calls it at line 2425.
findings.impact: Admins cannot create maker aliases for the new Pen, Pen Clip, or Refill product types even though the migration seeds their concepts; the create call throws Unsupported catalog product type. Any alias row in a non product-type namespace, which the schema now permits, makes listTerminologyAliases throw for every caller. Rows that pass the key check are returned with canonicalNamespace hardcoded to product-type regardless of their real namespace.
findings.recommendation: Filter the list query to canonicalNamespace = product-type until other namespaces are supported, and add the new pen slugs to the CatalogProductType union or carry the concept key as a plain string for the new types.

findings.title: Pen and spinner detail rows can mix on one product or collection item
findings.evidence: validate_pens_collection_detail counts only the six collection_detail_pen tables (lines 780 to 787) and validate_pens_product_detail counts only pen family tables. The fresh baseline seed shows products of an unrelated type accepting product_detail_spinner rows, so no visible constraint rejects cross family details. collection_catalog_product unions all detail families with LIMIT 1 and no ORDER BY (lines 918 to 931).
findings.impact: A collection item or product can hold detail rows from both the pen family and the spinner or slider family. The catalog product mapping then returns an arbitrary one of the two products, so configuration selection validation checks the wrong product and pages can show mixed subtype data.
findings.recommendation: Extend both validators to also count the pre-existing spinner and slider detail tables, or add one shared exactly-one-detail constraint across all families. Give collection_catalog_product a deterministic order or raise when more than one family matches.

findings.title: Collection selection trigger and several rule rejections have no tests
findings.evidence: The suite covers subtype deferral, required slots, rule ordering, market cycles, and evidence support. No test inserts into collection_item_configuration_selection, so validate_collection_configuration_selections (installed part owner match, single install, slot product match) is untested. No test rejects a choice whose carrier does not match its slot kind, and no test rejects two rules with the same requirement set even though the third test title says it does.
findings.impact: The most complex trigger in the migration can break silently. The carrier kind check, the duplicate rule signature check, and the whole owned part installation flow have no test that fails when they break.
findings.recommendation: Add rejection cases: a material choice in an appearance slot, a second rule for the same target with the same requirement set, a selection whose slot belongs to another product, an installed part owned by another user, and the same part installed twice.

findings.title: Global aliases are legal in the schema but invisible to the alias list
findings.evidence: The migration drops NOT NULL on catalog_terminology_alias.maker_id (line 566) and the new scope unique uses NULLS NOT DISTINCT, so global aliases are legal. listTerminologyAliases inner joins maker on alias.maker_id at line 3600, which drops those rows before the null guard at line 3609 can ever fire.
findings.impact: A legal global alias is invisible in the only list endpoint and the guard throw is dead code. The schema and the service disagree about whether global aliases exist.
findings.recommendation: Pick one side. If global aliases are planned, left join maker and make makerName nullable in the response. If not, keep maker_id NOT NULL and drop the nullsNotDistinct unique.

findings.title: Four redundant unique constraints add write cost with no integrity gain
findings.evidence: pens.ts declares four unique constraints already implied by narrower ones: product_configuration_choice_id_slot_product_unique at line 416, product_configuration_choice_rule_id_target_product_unique at line 472, refill_offering_market_status_id_scope_unique at line 980, and refill_offering_identifier_id_scope_unique at line 1058. Each includes the identity primary key column and no composite foreign key references these column sets.
findings.impact: Four extra unique indexes are maintained on every insert and update of the choice, rule, status, and identifier tables with no integrity gain.
findings.recommendation: Delete the four constraints from pens.ts and regenerate the migration. Keep only the key pairs that composite foreign keys actually reference.

dispositions.reason: The schema permits global aliases (maker_id NULL) via NULLS NOT DISTINCT, but the service query uses an INNER JOIN on maker, which excludes NULL maker_id rows entirely. Global aliases created in the database would be invisible to API consumers. The null guard throw at line 3609 is unreachable dead code.

dispositions.evidence: packages/database/src/schema/pens.ts:416 shows unique('product_configuration_choice_id_slot_product_unique') on (id, slotId, productId). review.overview:
Reviewer 1: PR #376 adds material Trends drill-downs to the Pocket-Trash application. The change introduces a new database table `public_collection_item_material_trend` for storing privacy-safe material aggregation data, adds two new service methods for retrieving exact catalog and collection-derived material counts, extends the existing Trends refresh job to populate material data, and adds UI components for filtering by general and specific materials with URL-persisted state. The implementation uses PostgreSQL grouping sets for efficient aggregation, maintains the existing privacy threshold of 5 contributors, and rounds counts to the nearest 5 before persistence.

Reviewer 2: This PR adds material drill-downs to the public Trends page. A new exact endpoint counts approved public catalog products by general material and specific alloy, and the existing privacy-safe refresh now also stores owned-item and collector counts per material, using the same 5-contributor threshold and round-to-five rule as the existing product-type trends. The page gains material and alloy selects driven by URL filters (materialId, materialSpecificId, productTypeId), three new chart-plus-table sections, and View products links to the materials pages. I read the diff plus the connected service, schema, migration, route, filter, and test evidence; assumed load is an anonymous public page with a periodic refresh.

findings.title: Missing newline at end of migration file
findings.evidence: The migration file ends without a trailing newline: `ALTER TABLE ... ON DELETE RESTRICT;\ No newline at end of file`
findings.impact: Minor - some tools may complain about missing trailing newline, but functionality is not affected.
findings.recommendation: Add a trailing newline to the migration file for consistency with other SQL files.

findings.title: material_specific is joined on id alone, contradicting the composite identity this change declares
findings.evidence: The catalog query joins left join material_specific on material_specific.id = scoped_products.material_specific_id (line 185), and the collection reader left joins materialSpecific on materialSpecific.id alone (lines 250-256). The new foreign key in packages/database/src/schema/trends.ts (lines 98-102) instead references material_specific(material_id, id), and every existing API in catalog-api.ts (product materialAssignments lines 398-402, saveAdminMaterialSpecific lines 1825-1831, moveAdminMaterialImage lines 1852-1859) identifies a specific by the materialId plus specificId pair.
findings.impact: If specific ids repeat across materials, as the composite foreign key and pair-based APIs imply, both queries fan out. The catalog grouping emits duplicate rows for one bucket with conflicting names and slugs, the collection reader returns one stored row many times with wrong labels, and the page renders duplicate React keys and wrong View products links. If ids are globally unique, the current joins happen to work.
findings.recommendation: Join on both columns in both queries: add and material_specific.material_id = scoped_products.material_id to the raw SQL, and pair the eq for the Drizzle left join. Also make filterMaterials in apps/web/src/pages/trends-page.tsx (line 233) require value.materialId === materialId when materialSpecificId is set.

findings.title: Collection material rows have no defined order; a test asserts one anyway
findings.evidence: The rows select in getPublicCollectionMaterialTrends (lines 226-262) has no orderBy, while sibling reads order by descending count then ascending name (lines 332-335). The integration test at packages/services/src/db/trends/index.integration.test.ts (lines 95-106) asserts an exact array order, Steel before Titanium, two rows with the same count 10.
findings.impact: Postgres may return equal-count rows in any order. That assertion can flake after a restore or plan change, and the page sorts only by count, so tied bars and rows can swap between page loads.
findings.recommendation: Add orderBy with descending roundedItemCount then ascending material and specific name, or sort once after mapping, and give the sort in filterMaterials a name tiebreaker.

findings.title: The material chart overflow bucket has no test
findings.evidence: MaterialTrendVisualization slices the top eight rows and sums the rest into a seeded Other row (lines 868-884). No test or story supplies more than two material rows.
findings.impact: The branch that collapses rows nine and beyond into Other is new branching logic on a public page. A regression in the seed or the sum, for example a mislabeled or duplicated Other bar, would pass CI today.
findings.recommendation: Add one render test with ten material rows asserting eight bars plus an Other bar with the summed count of the last two.

findings.title: Reader maps the same row twice for item and collector values
findings.evidence: collectorValues and itemValues (lines 264-287) repeat the same row-to-PublicMaterialTrend mapping, differing only in the count field.
findings.impact: Every new field must be added in two places, and a missed side silently drops data from one chart.
findings.recommendation: Map the rows once and derive the two value arrays by swapping the count field, or extract one mapper function.

findings.title: Refresh scans the eleven-table item union twice per run
findings.evidence: The material aggregation (lines 477-542) repeats the full item_products union over the eleven collection detail tables that the product-type aggregation at lines 427-439 already scans inside the same transaction.
findings.impact: Each refresh runs the heaviest scan twice. Refresh runs under an advisory lock roughly daily, so the cost is bounded, but it doubles the longest transaction.
findings.recommendation: Reuse one CTE for both aggregations in a single query pass, or keep the two queries if refresh time stays acceptable and the code reads clearer.

findings.title: Existing chart and table blocks duplicate the new material component
findings.evidence: MaterialTrendVisualization (lines 835-969) renders the same bar chart plus full-table pattern that the collection-item, collector, and part-accessory sections still implement inline (lines 585-699 and 756-812).
findings.impact: Four copies of the chart and table markup must now change together for any accessibility or styling fix.
findings.recommendation: Follow up by moving the three existing sections onto the shared component.

dispositions.evidence: packages/services/src/db/trends/index.ts:148-191 (review-evidence/13-content.txt): the GROUPING SETS query has no LIMIT; apps/web/src/lib/catalog-api.ts:1339-1344 and apps/web/src/routes/trends.tsx:30-51 return the full array with no pagination.
dispositions.reason: The evidence is accurate: the query really has no LIMIT and the whole result is returned. But the impact is unproven. Result size is driven by distinct (product type, material, specific variant) combinations, not by catalog size — a million pens over 50 materials still yields only a few hundred rows. Materials and variants are admin-curated, and nothing in the frozen source shows a taxonomy big enough for 'thousands of rows' or real memory pressure. Medium severity is not established by the frozen source; the real cost of this query is the live per-request aggregation, which the finding does not name.

dispositions.evidence: apps/web/src/pages/trends-page.tsx:227-239 (review-evidence/6-content.txt): filterMaterials matches the quoted nested ternary exactly. apps/web/src/lib/catalog-filters.ts:26-44 drops materialSpecificId unless materialId is valid; trends-page.tsx:302-307 resets materialSpecificId when the material changes; lines 210-220 build specific options only from rows of the selected material.
dispositions.reason: The quoted code exists, but the claimed impact does not hold. When both materialId and materialSpecificId are set, the specific-id branch is the intended drill-down: a specific id implies its parent material (enforced by the material_specific FK in migration.sql:19), and the UI can only produce consistent pairs. The one inconsistent case (a hand-crafted URL with a mismatched pair, which parseCatalogTrendsSearch does not cross-check) still shows rows matched by that specific id and labeled with their own specific name. No concrete wrong behavior is demonstrated, so this is a readability preference, not a medium-severity defect.

dispositions.evidence: apps/web/src/pages/trends-page.tsx:892-893 (review-evidence/6-content.txt): rowKey template matches the quote. PublicMaterialTrend IDs are number|null (packages/services/src/db/trends/index.ts:65-77) and are coerced with Number() at index.ts:192-206. The synthetic 'Other' row uses materialId: -1 (trends-page.tsx:876); migration.sql:15 enforces a unique scope index over (generation_id, coalesce(product_type_id,0), coalesce(material_id,0), coalesce(material_specific_id,0), is_specific_breakdown).
dispositions.reason: The collision precondition is impossible in the frozen source. IDs are numbers, so no ID can contain the ':' delimiter; the placeholders ('all', 'unspecified', 'general') are distinct fixed strings in fixed slots and cannot collide with numbers or each other; and each (productTypeId, materialId, materialSpecificId, isSpecificBreakdown) tuple is unique per row by the GROUP BY (catalog trends) or the unique index (collection trends). The 'Other' row's materialId -1 cannot collide with real ids or the null placeholder. The claimed risk is a factual error, not a low-severity nit.

dispositions.evidence: packages/services/src/db/trends/index.ts:L185 joins 'left join material_specific on material_specific.id = scoped_products.material_specific_id'; L250-256 joins on materialSpecific.id alone; packages/database/src/schema/trends.ts:L98-102 declares composite FK 'foreignKey({columns:[table.materialId,table.materialSpecificId],foreignColumns:[materialSpecific.materialId,materialSpecific.id]})'
dispositions.reason: The joins use only id, but the schema declares composite identity (material_id,id). If specific IDs repeat across materials, queries fan out: catalog returns duplicate rows with conflicting names, collection reader returns one row many times. Severity medium is supported.

dispositions.evidence: packages/services/src/db/trends/index.ts:L226-262 selects rows with no orderBy; L332-335 sibling query has 'orderBy(desc(...),asc(...))'; packages/services/src/db/trends/index.integration.test.ts:L95-106 asserts exact array order ['Steel','Titanium'] both with count 10
